An institution can also hold cash and still be insolvent if total asset value is below total obligations. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A balance-sheet resource can improve more than one resilience dimension, but the dimensions remain conceptually separate. ### Never confuse [Capital] and [Liquidity] **Capital** — loss-absorbing financial resources defined under accounting or prudential rules. --- **Liquidity** — capacity to meet cash and settlement obligations when they fall due. ### Never confuse [Equity] and [Regulatory capital] **Equity** — the accounting residual. --- **Regulatory capital** — the prudential measure after eligibility rules, deductions, and adjustments. ### Permanent trap Calling a bank “well capitalised” because it has a large cash balance. Cash is an asset; capital describes loss absorption. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Calibration and legal definitions vary, but capital, liquidity, and solvency remain distinct concepts in every jurisdiction.

title: The Financial Statements and How They Link
one_screen: Financial statements separate **position**, **performance**, **cash movement**, and **equity movement**. Profit can change equity without matching cash, financing can change cash without creating profit, and every recognised closing position ultimately appears in the closing balance sheet.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Statement / component | Owns | Time basis | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Balance sheet / statement of financial position | Assets · Liabilities · Equity | At a date | | Profit and loss / income statement | Recognised income · Expenses | Over a period | | Cash-flow statement | Cash receipts · Cash payments | Over a period | | Changes in equity | Movements among equity components | Over a period | “Three statements” is practitioner shorthand, not a claim that a complete statutory set contains only three documents. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Profit is not cash, and a cash movement is not automatically income or expense. Recognition and cash timing are separate questions. ### Never confuse [Profit] and [Cash flow] **Profit** — recognised income minus recognised expenses for a period. --- **Cash flow** — cash received or paid; accruals, non-cash items, financing, and investing transactions make it differ from profit. ### Permanent trap Forcing the change in cash to equal profit. Borrowing can increase cash and liabilities without income; impairment can reduce profit without an equal current-period cash payment. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Reporting boundary | | :--- | :--- | | IN | Commercial banks follow the Banking Regulation Act framework and RBI financial-statement directions; Ind AS should not be assumed for scheduled commercial banks. | | UK | Entities within scope use the applicable UK-adopted accounting framework, including UK-adopted international accounting standards where relevant. | | EU | Accounts within the IAS Regulation's scope use EU-adopted international accounting standards. | | US | Entities subject to US GAAP use the FASB Accounting Standards Codification under their applicable reporting requirements. |

title: Accrual Versus Cash
one_screen: Accrual accounting records the economic effects of events when the applicable recognition requirements are met, which can be earlier or later than cash settlement. The foundational discipline is simple: **recognition timing and cash timing are different dimensions.**
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Situation | Accounting effect | Cash effect at that moment | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Interest earned but not yet received | Income and an asset/carrying-amount effect can arise | None yet | | Expense incurred but not yet paid | Expense and liability can arise | None yet | | Cash paid before service is consumed | Asset/prepayment can arise | Cash decreases now | | Borrowing received | Cash and liability increase | Cash increases without profit | | Non-cash impairment recognised | Expense / carrying-value effect | No equal current cash payment | Accrual accounting does not mean “book whatever is expected”. Recognition and measurement must still follow the applicable accounting framework. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule The absence of a cash movement does not prove that no income, expense, asset, or liability should be recognised. ### Never confuse [Accrual] and [Cash settlement] **Accrual** — accounting recognition based on the economic event and applicable recognition rules. --- **Cash settlement** — transfer of cash; its date can differ from the recognition date. ### Permanent trap Rejecting a valid non-cash expense because “nothing has been paid yet”. Accounting can recognise deterioration or consumption before the related cash consequence is realised. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Specific recognition rules differ between accounting frameworks, but the distinction between accrual recognition and cash timing is universal.

title: Credit-Loss Allowances and Provisions
one_screen: Credit-loss accounting and prudential provisioning recognise that contractual claims may not be fully collected, but they are **not one universal calculation**. Recognition trigger, horizon, measurement, terminology, and prudential interaction come from the governing framework.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Event | Reporting effect | | :--- | :--- | | Credit exposure exists | Contractual claim is recognised | | Loss estimate changes | Governing framework measures the change | | Allowance / provision changes | Carrying amount and/or liability changes as required | | Charge / release recognised | Profit or loss changes under the applicable rules | The allowance is not cash placed in a separate reserve. Under US CECL, the allowance for applicable amortised-cost assets is a valuation account; under IFRS 9, impairment distinguishes 12-month and lifetime expected credit losses. Indian scheduled commercial banks sit under a different RBI provisioning framework. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Typical responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Finance / accounting | Record allowance and statement effect | | Credit risk / modelling | Supply governed inputs where required | | Management / committees | Approve material estimates and judgements | | Assurance | Challenge controls, evidence, methodology, reporting | ### Permanent rule An allowance or provision is a recognised measurement or prudential amount, not a segregated pot of cash. ### Never confuse [Accounting allowance] and [Prudential provision] **Accounting allowance** — credit-loss recognition under the applicable financial-reporting framework. --- **Prudential provision** — an amount required or recognised under supervisory rules; interaction does not make the two calculations identical. ### Permanent trap Assuming that “expected loss”, “provision”, “stage”, or “allowance” carries identical mechanics across jurisdictions. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Real delta | | :--- | :--- | | IN | RBI deferred Ind AS for scheduled commercial banks until further notice. Bank asset classification and provisioning follow RBI directions, including the 2025 IRACP Directions. | | UK | Entities applying UK-adopted IFRS 9 use the IFRS 9 expected-credit-loss model. | | EU | Accounts within EU-adopted IFRS scope use adopted IFRS 9 impairment requirements. | | US | ASC Topic 326 uses the CECL objective for applicable assets; no single estimation technique is universally mandated. |

title: Profit, OCI and Equity
one_screen: Recognised gains and losses do not all have to travel through current profit or loss. Accounting frameworks can require specified items to be presented in **other comprehensive income (OCI)** or another reserve route, but that route exists because the governing framework prescribes it—not because management prefers less earnings volatility.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Route | Current-period effect | Where accumulation appears | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Profit or loss | Included in current profit | Retained earnings after closing and distributions | | OCI under an applicable IFRS/US GAAP requirement | Outside current profit or loss | Accumulated within equity, subject to the framework | | Direct reserve/equity route under another framework | Depends on governing rule | Relevant reserve within equity | Some OCI items are later **reclassified** (“recycled”) into profit or loss when the relevant standard requires it; others are not. The instrument and governing rule determine the treatment. India requires a naming discipline: the RBI **AFS-Reserve** used for commercial-bank investment valuation is a prescribed reserve mechanism. It should not automatically be relabelled “IFRS 9 OCI”. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Management preference cannot create OCI eligibility. Presentation follows the applicable accounting or regulatory framework. ### Never confuse [OCI] and [Any reserve outside P&L] **OCI** — a defined financial-reporting category under frameworks that use it. --- **Other reserve** — a separately prescribed equity route that may have different recognition and recycling mechanics. ### Permanent trap Calling every valuation movement outside profit or loss “OCI”. That collapses distinct accounting and regulatory mechanisms into one label. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) RBI's 2025 commercial-bank investment directions prescribe an **AFS-Reserve** for qualifying AFS valuation gains and losses rather than routing those movements through profit or loss. Debt-instrument amounts are transferred to profit or loss on sale or maturity; designated equity treatment differs. #### UK UK-adopted international accounting standards use the IFRS architecture of profit or loss and OCI for entities applying that framework. #### EU EU-adopted IFRS uses the same architecture for accounts within scope. #### US US GAAP contains comprehensive-income and accumulated-OCI requirements, but the qualifying items and reclassification rules come from US GAAP, not IFRS.

title: How to Read a Bank Balance Sheet
one_screen: A bank balance sheet should be read as a funded risk position, not as a list of totals. The efficient sequence is **assets → funding → loss absorption → quality → maturity → concentration**, because each step asks what the preceding number actually means.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Pass | Question | What to inspect | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | 1. Assets | What does the bank own or have claims on? | Cash, securities, loans, other assets | | 2. Funding | Who finances those assets and on what terms? | Deposits, wholesale funding, other liabilities | | 3. Loss absorption | What residual / eligible capital sits beneath liabilities? | Equity and prudential-capital disclosures | | 4. Quality | How reliable are the carrying values and cash flows? | Credit quality, impairment, valuation | | 5. Maturity | When do assets turn into cash versus liabilities fall due? | Contractual and behavioural maturity | | 6. Concentration | What could fail together? | Counterparty, sector, geography, product, funding source | Equal totals can conceal radically different risk. Two banks with the same loan balance can have different borrower quality; two banks with the same deposits can have different deposit stability; two banks with the same equity can have different risk intensity. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Never infer resilience from a balance-sheet total without reading composition, quality, timing, and concentration. ### Never confuse [Book equity] and [Regulatory capital] **Book equity** — accounting residual. --- **Regulatory capital** — prudentially eligible capital after regulatory definitions and adjustments. ### Permanent trap Reading “large deposits” as “large liquidity”. Deposits are liabilities; the liquidity question concerns assets and funding behaviour under payment pressure. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Line-item names and disclosure templates differ, but this analytical sequence is jurisdiction-neutral.

title: Present Value and Discount Factors
one_screen: Present value puts cash flows occurring at different dates onto one valuation date. A **discount factor** is the multiplier that translates a future amount backward through time; the mathematics changes value for timing, not for whether the cash flow will occur.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism For a future cash flow CF_t, annual discount rate r, and t annual periods: ### Formula ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Cash flows at different dates are not economically comparable until their timing is put on a common basis. ### Never confuse [Discount rate] and [Discount factor] **Discount rate** — the rate input used to translate value through time. --- **Discount factor** — the numerical multiplier generated from the rate and timing. ### Never confuse [Discounting] and [Probability weighting] **Discounting** — adjusts for timing. --- **Probability weighting** — adjusts for uncertainty across outcomes. ### Permanent trap Using an annual rate as though each monthly cash flow were one full annual period. Correct algebra with mismatched units still produces a wrong valuation. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Present-value mathematics is universal; frameworks differ only in which cash flows and rate they instruct the user to apply.

title: Compounding, Rates and Timing Conventions
one_screen: Compounding moves value forward; discounting moves it backward. The formulas are simple, but financial models fail when the **rate frequency, compounding convention, cash-flow dates, and period count are inconsistent**.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism ### Formula ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Never apply a rate until its unit of time and compounding convention are consistent with the cash-flow timeline. ### Never confuse [Nominal annual rate] and [Effective annual rate] **Nominal annual rate** — an annualised quote whose realised one-year growth depends on the stated intra-year compounding convention. --- **Effective annual rate** — the actual one-year growth rate after the convention is reflected. ### Permanent trap Multiplying or dividing an annual rate by 12 without checking what the quoted rate means. Some conversions are simple only under a stated convention; others require compounding logic. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** These are mathematical identities and consistency requirements.

title: Effective Interest Rate
one_screen: The effective interest rate (EIR) is the single rate that makes the present value of a specified future cash-flow stream equal to a specified carrying amount or price. It compresses amount, timing, interest, and qualifying fees or costs into one internally consistent yield **for the cash-flow definition being used**.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism ### Formula ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule EIR has meaning only with a specified cash-flow definition. Change the included cash flows or timing and the solved rate can change. ### Never confuse [Coupon rate] and [Effective interest rate] **Coupon rate** — contractual rate or formula used to determine stated interest payments. --- **Effective interest rate** — the rate solving the relevant present-value equation. ### Never confuse [Effective interest rate] and [Current market yield] **Effective interest rate** — rate defined by the specified initial carrying amount and cash flows. --- **Current market yield** — return implied by today's market price and expectations; it can move after origination. ### Permanent trap Using the contractual coupon as EIR without checking price, fees, transaction costs, premiums, discounts, or payment timing. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The rate-solving mathematics is universal. Accounting frameworks determine the exact cash-flow set and how a resulting EIR is subsequently used.

title: NPV and Discounted Cash Shortfalls
one_screen: Net present value (NPV) aggregates dated amounts only after translating them to one valuation date. When a loss methodology discounts expected cash shortfalls, **probability determines how much is expected; discounting determines what the timing of that expected amount is worth today.**
bodyText: ### Core mechanism ### Formula ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Do not mix uncertainty and time value into one unexplained adjustment. They are separate operations even when one framework embeds both in a single measurement process. ### Never confuse [Nominal shortfall] and [Present value of shortfall] **Nominal shortfall** — difference in cash amounts at the future date. --- **Present value of shortfall** — that amount translated to the valuation date under the applicable discount rule. ### Permanent trap Exporting one framework's discounting rule into another framework because both use “expected credit loss” language. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Scheduled commercial-bank provisioning follows RBI prudential directions rather than an assumption that IFRS 9 EIR discounting governs bank IRACP provisioning. #### UK For entities applying UK-adopted IFRS 9, expected credit losses are discounted to the reporting date using the EIR determined at initial recognition or an approximation, subject to IFRS 9's instrument-specific rules. #### EU The same IFRS 9 principle applies where EU-adopted IFRS 9 governs the accounts. #### US CECL permits multiple reasonable estimation methods that achieve the Topic 326 objective; a discounted-cash-flow method is not mandatory in every case.

title: Probability and Expected Value
one_screen: Probability describes likelihood; expected value converts a set of possible numerical outcomes into their probability-weighted average. An expected value is a property of a modelled distribution—not a promise that the next realised outcome will equal that average.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism ### Formula ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule An expected value summarises a distribution. It does not identify which outcome will occur next. ### Never confuse [Probability] and [Expected amount] **Probability** — likelihood assigned to an event. --- **Expected amount** — probability-weighted numerical outcome. ### Permanent trap Reading a 1% chance of losing 100 as “the loss is 1%”. Likelihood and loss amount have different units and answer different questions. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Probability and expected-value mathematics are universal.

title: Variance, Standard Deviation and Volatility
one_screen: Expected value describes the centre of a distribution; variance describes how dispersed outcomes are around that centre. Standard deviation is the square root of variance, and in finance **volatility** usually refers to a standard-deviation measure whose meaning depends on the variable, observation frequency, and horizon.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism ### Formula ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A volatility number is incomplete without the underlying variable and its time horizon. ### Never confuse [Variance] and [Standard deviation] **Variance** — squared dispersion around the mean. --- **Standard deviation** — square root of variance, restoring the variable's units. ### Never confuse [Volatility] and [Downside loss] **Volatility** — dispersion in both directions under the chosen measure. --- **Downside loss** — adverse outcome; high positive outcomes can raise volatility without being losses. ### Permanent trap Comparing daily and annual volatility as if they were the same object merely because both are percentages. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** These statistical relationships do not vary by jurisdiction.

title: Quantiles and Tail Risk
one_screen: A quantile is a threshold in a distribution associated with a cumulative probability. Tail risk concerns the outcomes beyond an extreme threshold, so a high quantile can locate the edge of a tail without telling you how severe the tail becomes.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Let L be a loss variable. A 99th-percentile loss quantile is a level at or below which approximately 99% of modelled loss outcomes fall under the stated convention, leaving approximately 1% beyond it in a continuous setting. Two distributions can share the same 99% quantile while having radically different outcomes in the worst 1%. The quantile therefore answers **where the tail begins for the chosen probability level**, not **how bad every tail outcome is**. | Change | Effect on interpretation | | :--- | :--- | | Confidence level changes | Threshold changes | | Horizon changes | Distribution changes | | Model/data changes | Estimated threshold can change | | Tail shape changes | Severity beyond threshold can change even if quantile is similar | ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A quantile is a distribution threshold, never a hard cap on possible outcomes. ### Never confuse [Quantile] and [Maximum loss] **Quantile** — threshold associated with a cumulative probability. --- **Maximum loss** — greatest possible or defined loss under a separate assumption; it is not implied by a percentile. ### Never confuse [High confidence] and [Low probability of any loss] **High-confidence quantile** — leaves a small probability of outcomes beyond the stated threshold. --- **Probability of any loss** — probability that loss is greater than zero, which is a different question. ### Permanent trap Saying a 99% loss quantile means “there is only a 1% chance of losing money”. It means roughly 1% of modelled outcomes exceed that particular loss threshold. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Quantiles and probability tails are mathematical concepts.

title: Exposure: What Is Actually at Risk
one_screen: Exposure is the amount or position subject to adverse change from a specified risk event; it is **not the loss itself**. For credit, today's drawn balance can be only part of what is at risk because a facility may also contain undrawn commitments that can become exposure before the relevant event.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Facility component | What it means | | :--- | :--- | | Drawn amount | Amount already advanced or otherwise outstanding | | Undrawn commitment | Contractual capacity not yet drawn | | Total commitment | Drawn plus undrawn contractual amount | | Exposure measure | Amount treated as at risk under the stated purpose and measurement date | ### Formula ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Exposure is an input to loss measurement. It is never automatically equal to realised or expected loss. ### Never confuse [Exposure] and [Loss] **Exposure** — amount or position subject to the specified risk event. --- **Loss** — adverse outcome after the event under the relevant loss definition; foundations does not own the downstream severity mechanics. ### Never confuse [Drawn amount] and [Total commitment] **Drawn amount** — already used. --- **Total commitment** — drawn plus contractual undrawn capacity; downstream methods decide how much undrawn capacity enters a risk exposure measure. ### Permanent trap Using current outstanding principal as the complete exposure for a revolving or committed facility without checking whether further drawings can occur before the measurement event. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Specific regulatory exposure definitions and conversion factors can differ, but the distinction between amount at risk, current drawings, and contractual undrawn capacity is universal.

title: Expected Loss Versus Unexpected Loss
one_screen: Expected loss is the probability-weighted average loss at the centre of a modelled loss distribution; unexpected loss is the adverse variation around that expectation for which additional resilience may be needed. A low average loss can coexist with a dangerous tail.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Return to the two-state example: loss 100 with 1% probability, otherwise zero. Expected loss is 1, but the adverse realised state is 100. The difference between the distribution's average and materially worse outcomes creates the intuition for unexpected loss. ### Formula ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Planning for the average is not resilience. Risk management must also consider outcomes materially worse than the expected value. ### Never confuse [Expected loss] and [Most likely loss] **Expected loss** — probability-weighted mean. --- **Most likely loss** — mode or most probable outcome; it can differ sharply from the mean. ### Never confuse [Unexpected loss] and [One universal formula] ### Permanent trap Taking a high loss quantile, subtracting expected loss, and treating the result as a universally defined “unexpected loss” measure without checking the framework. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The statistical distinction is universal. Prudential and accounting frameworks decide how expected losses, provisions, and capital interact.

title: Risk Capacity, Appetite, Limits and Profile
one_screen: Risk governance turns resilience into choices. **Risk capacity** is how much risk the institution can bear; **risk appetite** is how much and what types it chooses to take within that capacity; **limits** translate appetite into operating boundaries; **risk profile** is the risk actually being run.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Layer | Question | | :--- | :--- | | Capacity | What is the maximum risk the institution can bear before binding constraints or viability are threatened? | | Appetite | What risk is it willing to assume in pursuing objectives? | | Limits | What measurable or enforceable boundaries convert appetite into decisions? | | Risk profile | What risk is actually being taken now? | | Escalation | What happens when profile approaches or breaches limits? | Capacity should bound appetite. Appetite should drive limits. Limits should influence decisions. Monitoring should compare the resulting profile with the approved boundaries. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Produces / owns | | :--- | :--- | | Governing body / board | Approves appetite and oversees alignment with strategy and capacity | | Senior management | Implements appetite and allocates limits | | Business management | Operates within limits and owns resulting risk | | Risk function | Framework, aggregation, monitoring, challenge, escalation | | Internal audit | Independent assurance over governance and controls | ### Permanent rule Appetite must sit within capacity, and appetite that cannot be translated into decisions, limits, or escalation is not operational. ### Never confuse [Risk capacity] and [Risk appetite] **Risk capacity** — maximum bearable risk subject to binding constraints. --- **Risk appetite** — chosen risk-taking within that capacity. ### Never confuse [Risk appetite] and [Risk profile] **Risk appetite** — desired boundary. --- **Risk profile** — actual risk being run. ### Permanent trap Raising a limit after a breach solely to make the breach disappear. A limit change is itself a governed risk decision and must be justified as such. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Supervisory expectations differ in detail, but the capacity–appetite–limits–profile architecture is cross-jurisdictional.

title: The Three Lines Model
one_screen: The Three Lines Model separates **management's action and ownership of risk**, specialist management support and challenge, and **independent internal-audit assurance**. It is a model of roles and accountability, not a rigid organisation chart and not permission for one line to outsource responsibility to another.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Role | Core contribution | | :--- | :--- | | Governing body | Oversight, direction, accountability to stakeholders | | First-line roles | Deliver products/services and manage the risks arising from activity | | Second-line roles | Expertise, support, monitoring, and challenge on risk-related matters | | Third-line / internal audit | Independent and objective assurance and advice | | External assurance providers | Additional assurance under their own mandates | First- and second-line roles are both management roles. Internal audit is qualitatively different because its independence from management responsibilities supports objective assurance. The IIA refreshed its Statement of Position on the Three Lines Model in July 2026. The current model continues to emphasise clear accountability, internal-audit independence, and useful coordination among assurance providers. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Question | Primary answer | | :--- | :--- | | Who owns business risk? | Management / first-line roles | | Who supports and challenges management? | Second-line roles | | Who independently assures governance and control? | Internal audit / third line | | Who oversees the whole structure? | Governing body | ### Permanent rule Management retains responsibility for managing risk. Internal audit must preserve the independence and objectivity required to assure that management system. ### Never confuse [Second line] and [Third line] **Second line** — management roles providing expertise, support, monitoring, and challenge. --- **Third line** — internal audit providing independent and objective assurance and advice. ### Permanent trap Calling a control failure “Risk's problem” merely because the second line monitors it. Monitoring does not transfer first-line ownership of the underlying activity and control. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The Three Lines Model is a governance model, not a jurisdiction-specific banking rule. Local laws and supervisory rules can add role-specific requirements.

title: Policy, Standard, Procedure and Evidence
one_screen: A useful internal-governance hierarchy is **policy → standard → procedure → evidence**: intent and mandatory outcomes become testable requirements, then execution steps, then proof that the steps occurred. The labels are not legally universal, so authority, scope, approval, and content matter more than the filename.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Layer | Owns | Test | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Policy | Intent, principles, mandatory outcomes, boundaries | What must be true? | | Standard | Detailed mandatory criteria and control requirements | What exact requirement must be met? | | Procedure | Operational sequence | How is the requirement performed? | | Evidence / record | Proof of execution and decision | Can performance be demonstrated? | A procedure cannot legitimately authorise something prohibited by its governing policy. A standard cannot silently widen a board-approved risk boundary. Lower-level documents implement higher-authority requirements; they do not override them. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Typical responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Governing body / delegated authority | Approves highest-level policies within governance | | Policy owner | Maintains content, scope, and review cycle | | Control / standard owner | Defines testable mandatory requirements | | Process owner | Maintains procedures and executes controls | | Risk / compliance | Challenges framework and monitors within remit | | Internal audit | Independently assesses design and operation | ### Permanent rule Authority flows downward; evidence flows upward. Execution must be traceable to a valid requirement, and assurance must be able to trace the requirement to evidence. ### Never confuse [Document title] and [Document authority] **Document title** — label such as policy, standard, framework, or manual. --- **Document authority** — who approved it, what it governs, and whether it is mandatory. ### Never confuse [Procedure] and [Evidence] **Procedure** — steps that should be performed. --- **Evidence** — proof that the steps and required decisions actually occurred. ### Permanent trap Treating a beautifully written procedure as proof of control effectiveness. A procedure describes intended execution; evidence and testing show whether it happened. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Institutions and regulators use different terminology, but no universal statutory taxonomy fixes these four labels across jurisdictions.

title: What Regulators and Supervisors Actually Do
one_screen: **Regulation sets applicable requirements; supervision tests institutions against those requirements and supervisory objectives.** Authorisation, reporting, examination, remediation, and enforcement surround that core according to each authority's legal mandate.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Function | Question answered | | :--- | :--- | | Statutory mandate | What powers and objectives exist? | | Regulation / rulemaking | What requirements apply? | | Authorisation | Who may conduct regulated activity? | | Reporting | What information must firms provide? | | Supervision / examination | What is actually happening inside the firm? | | Remediation / enforcement | What must change, and what consequences are available? | A minimum ratio is only one supervisory input. Supervisors can also assess governance, controls, risk concentrations, data, financial condition, and management capability. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A regulator's title does not reveal its full mandate. Identify the entity supervised, legal power, and function being exercised. ### Never confuse [Regulation] and [Supervision] **Regulation** — establishes applicable requirements under the relevant mandate. --- **Supervision** — assesses firms and practices against requirements and supervisory objectives. ### Permanent trap Treating a reported ratio above minimum as proof that supervisory concern is impossible. Point-in-time compliance does not settle governance, controls, concentrations, or resilience. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Supervisory architecture | | :--- | :--- | | IN | RBI exercises banking regulation and supervision within its statutory remit, including directions, reporting, inspection, and enforcement. | | UK | PRA prudentially regulates and supervises firms within remit; FCA has major conduct responsibilities and prudential responsibilities for firms within its remit. | | EU | EBA develops harmonised rules and convergence; ECB/SSM and national competent authorities supervise institutions according to remit. | | US | Supervision is multi-agency; Federal Reserve, OCC, FDIC, and state authorities cover institutions according to charter and statute. |

title: Prudential, Conduct and Accounting Frameworks
one_screen: Prudential, conduct, and accounting frameworks can govern the same bank because they answer different questions. Their outputs interact; compliance in one never proves compliance in another.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Framework | Question | Outputs | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Prudential | Can the institution remain safe, sound, resilient? | Capital · Liquidity · Governance · Risk requirements | | Conduct | Is behaviour proper toward customers and markets? | Product · Disclosure · Sales · Market-conduct obligations | | Accounting | How are economic events reported? | Recognition · Measurement · Presentation · Disclosure | One item can cross all three: a credit-loss allowance affects accounting profit/equity; prudential rules determine regulatory treatment; conduct rules can govern the underlying product or servicing. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Never carry a label or treatment from one framework into another without checking the governing rule. ### Never confuse [Prudential regulation] and [Accounting standards] **Prudential regulation** — safety, soundness, resilience, supervision. --- **Accounting standards** — financial-statement recognition, measurement, presentation, disclosure. ### Never confuse [Prudential regulation] and [Conduct regulation] **Prudential regulation** — whether the institution can safely bear and manage risk. --- **Conduct regulation** — whether behaviour meets customer and market obligations. ### Permanent trap Assuming an accounting allowance, reserve, or valuation label fixes regulatory-capital treatment. Prudential rules can adjust accounting inputs. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Boundary | | :--- | :--- | | IN | RBI carries major banking prudential and conduct-related roles. Scheduled commercial-bank reporting/provisioning follows the RBI framework; Ind AS 109 should not be assumed. | | UK | PRA is principal prudential regulator within remit; FCA is principal conduct regulator and also has prudential responsibilities within remit; accounting standards are separate. | | EU | CRR/CRD/EBA form core prudential architecture; ECB/SSM and national authorities supervise by remit; EU-adopted IFRS is separate for accounts within scope. | | US | Federal/state prudential oversight is split by charter/activity; banking agencies also enforce specified consumer rules; FASB sets US GAAP, not bank supervision. |

title: Impairment, Allowance and Write-off
one_screen: Impairment recognises that a financial asset is not expected to deliver all contractual value. The loss allowance measures expected non-collection; it changes accounting measurement without, by itself, changing what the borrower legally owes.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Object | What happens | What does not happen | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Gross carrying amount | Contractual asset remains recorded | Borrower debt is not automatically forgiven | | Loss allowance | Expected credit loss is recognised | It is not a pool of capital | | Net carrying amount | Asset is shown net of allowance where the framework requires | Contract is not extinguished | | Impairment gain/loss | Change in allowance affects earnings where required | It is not the same as a cash loss | | Write-off | Gross asset and allowance are reduced when recovery is no longer reasonably expected | Enforcement rights need not always disappear | Performing exposure → expected loss can still exist → allowance recognised Default → expected loss usually rises → allowance rises No reasonable expectation of recovery → write-off ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Impairment measures expected recoverability. It does not by itself cancel the contractual claim. ### Never confuse [Loss allowance] and [Capital] **Loss allowance** — a measured reduction in the carrying amount, or a provision for an off-balance-sheet exposure, reflecting expected credit loss. --- **Capital** — loss-absorbing financial resource supporting the institution against losses, including unexpected loss. They are different objects and are not substitutes. ### Never confuse [Impairment] and [Default] **Impairment** — accounting or prudential recognition of expected credit loss. --- **Default** — a governed credit-risk state of an obligor or facility. Impairment can exist before default. ### Permanent trap “Performing” does not mean “zero allowance”. Expected-loss frameworks recognise credit loss before a borrower necessarily becomes delinquent or defaults. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Commercial banks currently use RBI’s IRACP provisioning regime; the separate RBI ECL framework starts on 1 April 2027. Ind AS-implementing NBFCs and ARCs apply Ind AS impairment subject to RBI prudential guidance. #### UK (UKEB) No accounting-mechanics delta: UK-adopted IFRS 9 applies the expected-credit-loss model. #### EU (European Commission) No accounting-mechanics delta: EU-adopted IFRS 9 applies, with EBA supervisory guidance for credit institutions. #### US (FASB) ASC 326 uses an allowance for credit losses but generally measures lifetime expected losses for in-scope amortised-cost assets from initial recognition.

title: Three Expected-Loss Architectures
one_screen: IFRS 9, US CECL and RBI provisioning answer the same economic question—how much credit loss should be recognised now—but they do not use the same recognition architecture. Learn the framework before learning the calculation.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Framework | Initial performing exposure | Deteriorated exposure | Credit-impaired/defaulted exposure | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | IFRS 9 | Stage 1: 12-month ECL | Stage 2: lifetime ECL after SICR | Stage 3: lifetime ECL | | US CECL | Lifetime expected loss | Re-estimated lifetime loss | Re-estimated lifetime loss | | RBI commercial banks: current | IRACP classification and prescribed provisioning | IRACP rules | NPA classification and prescribed provisioning | | RBI commercial banks: from 1 Apr 2027 | Stage 1: 12-month ECL, subject to prudential floors | Stage 2: lifetime ECL | Stage 3: lifetime ECL, with NPA rules retained | | Ind AS-implementing NBFCs / ARCs | Ind AS 109 ECL | Ind AS 109 ECL | Ind AS 109 ECL, plus RBI prudential safeguards | ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Similar terminology does not make two frameworks equivalent. Recognition horizon, staging, scope and prudential floors can create materially different allowances on the same economics. ### Never confuse [Accounting standard] and [Prudential provisioning regime] **Accounting standard** — determines financial-statement recognition and measurement. --- **Prudential provisioning regime** — regulatory requirements designed for safety and soundness, which may prescribe floors or classifications beyond accounting measurement. ### Permanent trap Calling CECL “IFRS 9 without stage labels” misses the central difference: CECL generally recognises lifetime expected loss from initial recognition instead of waiting for SICR. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Three tracks coexist: current bank IRACP, Ind AS for applicable NBFCs/ARCs, and the final RBI bank ECL framework effective 1 April 2027. #### UK (UKEB) UK-adopted IFRS 9 supplies the accounting architecture. #### EU (European Commission / EBA) EU-adopted IFRS 9 supplies accounting measurement; EBA guidance overlays supervisory expectations. #### US (FASB) ASC 326 CECL uses lifetime expected-loss recognition for in-scope amortised-cost assets without an IFRS 9 SICR gateway.

title: Scope and Financial-Statement Presentation
one_screen: Before measuring ECL, determine whether the instrument is inside the impairment model and where the allowance is presented. The same expected-loss idea can appear as a deduction from an asset, an OCI amount or a separate provision depending on the instrument.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | IFRS 9 exposure | ECL treatment | Presentation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Debt asset at amortised cost | In scope | Loss allowance reduces carrying amount | | Debt asset at FVOCI | In scope | Allowance recognised in OCI; fair-value carrying amount is not reduced | | Loan commitment in scope | In scope | Provision rather than asset deduction | | Financial guarantee contract in scope | In scope | Provision rather than asset deduction | | Trade receivable / contract asset | In scope | Simplified lifetime-ECL approach may apply | | Lease receivable | In scope | Simplified lifetime-ECL policy may apply | | Instrument at FVTPL | Generally outside ECL impairment model | Credit effects are reflected through fair-value measurement | ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Do not calculate an ECL allowance until the instrument’s accounting classification and impairment scope are known. ### Never confuse [FVOCI allowance] and [Asset carrying amount reduction] **FVOCI allowance** — credit loss is recognised through the impairment mechanism and OCI. --- **Asset carrying amount** — remains at fair value; the allowance does not reduce that reported fair-value amount. ### Permanent trap Applying ECL to every item labelled “credit exposure” ignores instruments whose credit risk is already captured through another measurement basis. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Current commercial-bank provisioning scope is governed by IRACP rather than IFRS 9 classification. From 1 April 2027, RBI’s bank ECL framework covers loans, investments, undrawn commitments and other specified credit exposures, with prudential floors. #### UK (UKEB) No delta from UK-adopted IFRS 9. #### EU (European Commission) No accounting delta from EU-adopted IFRS 9. #### US (FASB) ASC 326 applies CECL to financial assets measured at amortised cost and has separate credit-loss requirements for available-for-sale debt securities. Off-balance-sheet credit exposures are also addressed where the entity is exposed to credit risk.

title: Credit Loss as a Discounted Cash Shortfall
one_screen: Under IFRS 9, the accounting target is the present value of contractual cash that will not be collected, including loss caused by delayed collection. PD, LGD and EAD are ways to estimate that target; they are not its definition.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Input | Measurement role | | :--- | :--- | | Contractual cash flows | Establish what is due | | Expected borrower payments | Reduce the shortfall | | Eligible recoveries | Reduce the shortfall when expected to be realised | | Recovery timing and costs | Change present value of collections | | Effective interest rate | Discounts shortfalls to the reporting date | ### Flow ### Formula ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Timing is part of credit loss. Receiving the same nominal cash much later can still create a loss. ### Never confuse [Credit loss] and [Fair-value loss] **Credit loss** — expected contractual cash shortfall attributable to credit risk. --- **Fair-value loss** — market-value movement that can contain interest-rate, liquidity, credit and other effects. ### Permanent trap Treating PD × LGD × EAD as the accounting definition can make the implementation drive the objective. The model must reproduce the required loss concept, not redefine it. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Current commercial-bank IRACP is rule-based rather than an Ind AS 109 discounted-cash-shortfall model. RBI’s bank framework from 1 April 2027 introduces ECL measurement and EIR mechanics. #### UK (UKEB) No delta from IFRS 9. #### EU (European Commission) No delta from IFRS 9. #### US (FASB) CECL aims to reflect the net amount expected to be collected but permits several estimation techniques; discounted cash flow is not mandatory for every asset.

title: The IFRS 9 Three-Stage Architecture
one_screen: IFRS 9 changes the loss horizon as credit risk changes. Stage 1 carries 12-month ECL, Stage 2 carries lifetime ECL after significant deterioration, and Stage 3 carries lifetime ECL once the asset is credit-impaired.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Stage | Credit state | Allowance | Interest basis | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Stage 1 | No SICR since initial recognition, subject to applicable expedients | 12-month ECL | Gross carrying amount | | Stage 2 | SICR, but not credit-impaired | Lifetime ECL | Gross carrying amount | | Stage 3 | Credit-impaired | Lifetime ECL | Amortised cost for assets that became credit-impaired after origination | ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Stage is a credit-risk state that determines measurement treatment. It is not simply a delinquency band. ### Never confuse [Stage 2] and [Stage 3] **Stage 2** — credit risk has increased significantly since initial recognition, but the asset is not credit-impaired. --- **Stage 3** — events have occurred that detrimentally affect expected future cash flows. ### Permanent trap Mapping Stage 1 / 2 / 3 directly to 0–29 / 30–89 / 90+ DPD reverses the framework. Delinquency is evidence and backstop information; it is not the complete definition of the stages. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Commercial banks do not currently use the IFRS 9 stage model. RBI’s framework effective 1 April 2027 introduces Stage 1, Stage 2 and Stage 3 for provisioning while retaining separate NPA-classification rules. #### UK (UKEB) No delta from UK-adopted IFRS 9. #### EU (European Commission / EBA) No accounting delta from EU-adopted IFRS 9; EBA guidance adds supervisory expectations around sound implementation. #### US (FASB) CECL has no equivalent Stage 1-to-Stage 2 horizon switch for amortised-cost assets.

title: Twelve-Month ECL versus Lifetime ECL
one_screen: Twelve-month ECL is not twelve months of cash loss. It is the lifetime loss consequence of default events that are possible within the next twelve months; lifetime ECL instead considers defaults possible over the relevant remaining life.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Question | 12-month ECL | Lifetime ECL | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Which default events enter? | Defaults possible in next 12 months, or shorter remaining life | Defaults possible over relevant remaining life | | How much loss follows an included default? | Full discounted loss consequence | Full discounted loss consequence | | Can post-month-12 recoveries matter? | Yes | Yes | | Typical IFRS 9 use | Stage 1 | Stage 2 and Stage 3 | ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule “Twelve months” limits the default-event window, not the period over which resulting cash shortfalls and recoveries are measured. ### Never confuse [12-month ECL] and [Twelve months of losses] **12-month ECL** — lifetime consequences of defaults possible within the next twelve months. --- **Twelve months of losses** — only shortfalls occurring during the next year. That is not the IFRS 9 definition. ### Permanent trap Cutting off post-default recoveries or losses at month twelve understates or distorts Stage 1 ECL whenever workout continues beyond one year. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Current commercial-bank IRACP has no 12-month-ECL concept. RBI’s bank ECL framework from 1 April 2027 adopts 12-month ECL for Stage 1 and lifetime ECL for Stage 2 and Stage 3. #### UK (UKEB) No delta from IFRS 9. #### EU (European Commission) No delta from IFRS 9. #### US (FASB) CECL does not use a Stage 1 12-month allowance for amortised-cost assets; lifetime expected credit loss is recognised from initial recognition.

title: Significant Increase in Credit Risk
one_screen: SICR asks whether the risk of default has increased significantly since initial recognition. It is therefore principally a relative deterioration test, not a test of whether current risk has crossed one universal “bad borrower” threshold.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism CR-10 → PD = likelihood of default over a defined horizon. | Step | Question | | :--- | :--- | | 1 | What was default risk at initial recognition? | | 2 | What is default risk at the reporting date over the relevant remaining life? | | 3 | Has the increase become significant? | | 4 | Do qualitative, forward-looking or collective indicators change the conclusion? | | 5 | If yes: Stage 2 and lifetime ECL; if no: Stage 1, subject to other rules | ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule SICR measures deterioration from the risk accepted at initial recognition. ### Never confuse [Relative deterioration] and [Absolute high risk] **Relative deterioration** — how far risk has moved from the starting point. --- **Absolute high risk** — how risky the exposure is today. A low-risk origination can experience SICR before becoming absolutely high risk. ### Permanent trap One current-PD threshold for every exposure can miss severe deterioration in loans that began with very low risk and over-stage loans that were already risky at origination. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Current commercial-bank IRACP does not use IFRS 9 SICR. RBI’s bank framework from 1 April 2027 requires assessment of significant deterioration for Stage 2. Ind AS-implementing NBFCs apply Ind AS ECL subject to RBI guidance. #### UK (UKEB) No accounting delta from UK-adopted IFRS 9. #### EU (European Commission / EBA) No accounting delta from EU-adopted IFRS 9; EBA guidance expects timely identification of deterioration. #### US (FASB) CECL has no SICR gateway determining whether lifetime loss begins.

title: SICR Evidence, Backstops and Collective Assessment
one_screen: SICR must use reasonable and supportable information that becomes available before default. Delinquency is one signal; the more-than-30-DPD rule is a rebuttable backstop, while collective assessment catches deterioration that individual borrower data has not yet revealed.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Evidence | Role | | :--- | :--- | | Internal rating / PD migration | Quantifies deterioration | | Watchlist or covenant deterioration | Borrower-specific early warning | | Forbearance / restructuring | May indicate financial difficulty | | Sector or macro stress | Forward-looking deterioration | | More than 30 DPD | Rebuttable SICR presumption under IFRS 9 | | Shared risk characteristics | Supports collective SICR assessment | | Low credit risk at reporting date | IFRS 9 practical expedient where its conditions are met | ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A backstop catches deterioration that earlier information failed to identify. It does not replace earlier information. ### Never confuse [30-DPD presumption] and [Stage 2 definition] **30-DPD presumption** — a rebuttable backstop. --- **Stage 2 definition** — significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition. ### Permanent trap Waiting until day 31 before considering Stage 2 turns an early-recognition framework into a delinquency framework. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) For Ind AS-implementing NBFCs, RBI reinforces the more-than-30-DPD rebuttable presumption and requires that recognition of SICR not be deferred beyond 60 days past due. RBI’s commercial-bank ECL framework from 1 April 2027 also contains SICR backstops. #### UK (UKEB) No accounting delta from IFRS 9. #### EU (European Commission / EBA) No accounting delta; EBA guidance reinforces timely, forward-looking and collective assessment. #### US (FASB) No SICR or 30-DPD staging presumption exists under CECL, although delinquency remains relevant credit information.

title: Credit-Impaired Assets, Stage 3 and Interest
one_screen: Stage 3 means events have occurred that detrimentally affect expected future cash flows. It is more than elevated risk: lifetime ECL continues, and for assets that became credit-impaired after origination IFRS 9 also changes the base on which interest revenue is calculated.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Evidence of credit impairment can include | Why it matters | | :--- | :--- | | Significant borrower financial difficulty | Capacity to pay has weakened materially | | Breach such as default or serious delinquency | Contractual performance has failed | | Concession granted because of financial difficulty | Original cash flows are no longer expected | | Probable bankruptcy or financial reorganisation | Future collection is impaired | | Other detrimental event affecting expected cash flows | Substance governs, not one indicator | CR-03 → default is a governed credit event; it is not identical to Stage 3. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Leaving Stage 3 does not automatically mean Stage 1. Credit impairment may have cured while SICR relative to origination still remains. ### Never confuse [Stage 3] and [NPA] **Stage 3** — an IFRS 9 or similar ECL credit-impaired state. --- **NPA** — a prudential asset-classification status defined by the applicable regulator. They can be operationally related without being the same legal object. ### Permanent trap Treating 90 DPD as the universal definition of Stage 3 misses credit impairment that becomes evident earlier and confuses an operational default backstop with the accounting concept. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Current commercial-bank IRACP uses NPA, substandard, doubtful and loss classifications rather than IFRS Stage 3. RBI’s ECL framework from 1 April 2027 introduces Stage 3 while explicitly retaining NPA classification. #### UK (UKEB) No accounting delta from IFRS 9. #### EU (European Commission) No accounting delta from IFRS 9; prudential default remains a separate regulatory concept. #### US (FASB) CECL has no Stage 3 allowance category. US nonaccrual and regulatory classifications remain separate from Topic 326 measurement.

title: Purchased or Originated Credit-Impaired Assets
one_screen: A purchased or originated credit-impaired asset is already credit-impaired when first recognised. IFRS 9 therefore does not treat its initial expected loss as ordinary post-origination deterioration: the starting economics already incorporate impaired expected cash flows.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Ordinary asset | POCI asset | | :--- | :--- | | Not credit-impaired at initial recognition | Credit-impaired at initial recognition | | Ordinary EIR | Credit-adjusted EIR | | Stage migration can occur after origination | Initial impairment is embedded in starting economics | | Allowance reflects required ECL under staging | Subsequent cumulative change in lifetime ECL is recognised | ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule POCI starts from an impaired credit state; it is not an ordinary new asset that happens to be placed directly into Stage 3. ### Never confuse [POCI] and [Asset that later becomes Stage 3] **POCI** — credit-impaired when first recognised by the reporting entity. --- **Later Stage 3 asset** — not credit-impaired initially, but becomes credit-impaired after recognition. ### Permanent trap Adding a conventional Day-1 Stage 3 allowance on top of pricing that already reflects expected credit impairment can double-count the initial credit loss under IFRS 9. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Current commercial-bank IRACP has no Ind AS 109 POCI model. RBI’s bank ECL framework from 1 April 2027 separately identifies POCI-type treatment. Applicable Ind AS NBFCs follow Ind AS requirements. #### UK (UKEB) No delta from IFRS 9 POCI accounting. #### EU (European Commission) No delta from IFRS 9 POCI accounting. #### US (FASB) ASC 326 uses purchased credit deteriorated, or PCD, accounting. The acquisition-date allowance is added to purchase price to establish the initial amortised-cost basis: a different architecture from IFRS 9 POCI.

title: The ECL Engine: Period-by-Period Expected Loss
one_screen: A common ECL engine decomposes expected loss into default timing, exposure at that time, loss severity and discounting. The decomposition is useful only if its aggregate output remains consistent with the governing expected-cash-shortfall objective.
bodyText: ### Formula ### Core mechanism | Stage / framework | Default periods entering the engine | | :--- | :--- | | IFRS 9 Stage 1 | Defaults possible within next 12 months | | IFRS 9 Stage 2 | Defaults possible over remaining relevant life | | IFRS 9 Stage 3 | Lifetime expected cash shortfalls on credit-impaired asset | | CECL | Expected losses over applicable contractual term | | RBI bank ECL from 1 Apr 2027 | Stage-dependent 12-month / lifetime structure | ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule All model components must describe the same exposure, default definition, timing basis and economic scenario. ### Never confuse [ECL formula] and [Accounting definition] ### Permanent trap Mixing a lifetime PD with current EAD and one-year LGD, or mixing conditional and unconditional default probabilities, can create a number that looks precise but has no coherent probabilistic meaning. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Current commercial-bank IRACP does not require this engine. RBI’s framework from 1 April 2027 uses a general PD/LGD/EAD-style approach within its ECL requirements. #### UK (UKEB) IFRS 9 does not prescribe PD/LGD/EAD as the only permissible technique. #### EU (European Commission / EBA) Same accounting position as IFRS 9; EBA guidance focuses on sound implementation rather than one mandatory model form. #### US (FASB) CECL is method-neutral: PD/LGD is permitted but not mandatory.

title: PD Term Structures
one_screen: Lifetime ECL needs default risk distributed through time, not one undated lifetime percentage. Cumulative PD tells whether default has occurred by a horizon; marginal PD allocates that risk to one future interval; conditional PD measures default during that interval given survival to its start.
bodyText: ### Formula ### Core mechanism | Horizon | Cumulative PD | Marginal PD | | :--- | ---: | ---: | | Year 1 | 2% | 2% | | Year 2 | 5% | 3% | | Year 3 | 9% | 4% | The year-3 cumulative 9% already contains the earlier 2% and 3%. Adding 2% + 5% + 9% would repeatedly count the same defaults. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A borrower can newly default only once. Period default probabilities must therefore be mutually consistent. ### Never confuse [Cumulative PD] and [Marginal PD] **Cumulative PD** — probability of default by a horizon. --- **Marginal PD** — probability of default specifically within one future interval. ### Permanent trap Adding cumulative PDs across years double-counts defaults already included in earlier horizons. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Current IRACP does not require PD term structures. RBI’s bank ECL framework from 1 April 2027 requires 12-month and lifetime default-risk measurement appropriate to stage. #### UK (UKEB) No prescribed IFRS 9 term-structure methodology; the measurement objective governs. #### EU (European Commission / EBA) No accounting delta from IFRS 9. #### US (FASB) CECL permits PD-based methods but does not require them.

title: EAD Paths, Commitments and Revolving Life
one_screen: EAD is exposure at the future point of default, not today’s balance repeated through time. Amortisation, prepayment, redraws and commitments create an exposure path; revolving products can also make effective credit exposure outlive a simple contractual notice period.
bodyText: ### Formula ### Core mechanism | Facility | Main EAD question | | :--- | :--- | | Amortising term loan | How much principal remains at each date? | | Bullet loan | Does exposure remain high until maturity? | | Undrawn commitment | How much will be drawn before default? | | Revolving facility | How do drawdown, repayment, limit management and cancellation behave? | ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule EAD must correspond to the exposure expected at the same future default date represented by PD. ### Never confuse [Contractual notice period] and [Behavioural exposure period] **Contractual notice period** — legal period over which cancellation or repayment rights operate. --- **Behavioural exposure period** — period credit exposure is expected to persist given actual behaviour and risk-management actions. ### Permanent trap Using today’s balance for every future period ignores amortisation and stress-driven drawdown. Using a nominal cancellation right as the horizon without considering actual revolving behaviour can also understate risk. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) RBI’s bank ECL framework from 1 April 2027 addresses drawn and undrawn exposures and applies prudential floors to undrawn commitments after relevant conversion. #### UK (UKEB) IFRS 9 contains a specific exposure-period exception for qualifying revolving instruments whose credit exposure is not effectively limited by the contractual notice period. #### EU (European Commission) No accounting delta from IFRS 9. #### US (FASB) CECL considers the contractual exposure period for off-balance-sheet commitments; no allowance is recorded for commitments the institution can unconditionally cancel.

title: LGD, Recoveries and Collateral
one_screen: LGD translates default into loss severity. For accounting ECL it must represent expected discounted shortfall after relevant borrower payments, collateral or guarantee recoveries and workout costs; a prudential-capital LGD may be calibrated to a different objective.
bodyText: ### Formula ### Core mechanism Default ↓ Exposure to recover ↓ Borrower payments + collateral + guarantees ↓ Recovery timing and costs ↓ Discounted shortfall ↓ Accounting LGD ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Collateral changes loss severity, not the borrower’s underlying obligation to repay. ### Never confuse [Accounting LGD] and [Regulatory LGD] **Accounting LGD** — calibrated to the expected-loss measurement objective at the reporting date. --- **Regulatory LGD** — calibrated for prudential capital purposes and may incorporate downturn requirements, floors or other conservatism. A regulatory parameter can be a starting point. It is not automatically an accounting parameter. ### Permanent trap Copying a downturn regulatory LGD unchanged into accounting ECL can import prudential conservatism into a measurement that is supposed to be an unbiased expected outcome. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Current commercial-bank IRACP is not an accounting-LGD model. From 1 April 2027 banks will estimate ECL under RBI’s framework while also applying RBI prudential floors; the modelled loss and the regulatory minimum therefore remain distinct. #### UK (UKEB / PRA) IFRS 9 accounting LGD and prudential capital LGD have different objectives. #### EU (European Commission / EBA) Same accounting distinction; prudential IRB parameters remain governed separately from IFRS 9 ECL. #### US (FASB) CECL permits LGD-based approaches but does not prescribe them.

title: Forward-Looking Information and Scenarios
one_screen: Expected loss must respond to relevant future conditions, not only historical averages. Forward-looking information changes ECL through defensible links to default, exposure, recovery or staging, and probability weighting must capture material non-linearity rather than merely selecting one “most likely” macro path.
bodyText: ### Flow ### Formula ### Core mechanism | Design question | Required discipline | | :--- | :--- | | Which macro variables? | Use variables with defensible connection to portfolio credit outcomes | | How many scenarios? | Enough to capture material alternative outcomes and non-linearity | | How assign probabilities? | Governed economic judgement, not reverse-engineering a desired allowance | | What beyond supportable forecast horizon? | Use a disciplined extrapolation or reversion method | | Where does FLI enter? | PD, LGD, EAD, staging or combinations, without double-counting | ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Forward-looking information belongs in ECL through a demonstrable connection to expected credit outcomes. ### Never confuse [Forecast horizon] and [ECL horizon] **Forecast horizon** — period over which specific economic forecasts remain reasonable and supportable. --- **ECL horizon** — period over which the framework requires expected losses to be measured. The ECL horizon can be longer. ### Permanent trap Calculating ECL once using probability-weighted average macro inputs can miss non-linearity. Weighted inputs and weighted losses are not generally the same calculation. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Current commercial-bank IRACP is not a scenario-weighted ECL regime. RBI’s framework from 1 April 2027 requires forward-looking macroeconomic information and multiple scenarios. #### UK (UKEB) No accounting delta from IFRS 9. #### EU (European Commission / EBA) No accounting delta; EBA guidance reinforces robust forward-looking estimation. #### US (FASB) CECL incorporates historical experience, current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts, with reversion to historical information beyond the supportable forecast period.

title: Overlays and Management Judgement
one_screen: An overlay or post-model adjustment addresses material credit risk the core model does not capture adequately. It is a controlled correction for a named limitation, not a reserve used to move the allowance toward a preferred number.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Condition | Action | | :--- | :--- | | Risk adequately captured | No overlay | | New risk outside model boundary | Quantify residual impact | | Structural break weakens calibration | Temporary adjustment + remediation | | Same risk already enters scenario PD/LGD/EAD | Do not count again | | Model repaired or risk disappears | Reduce or remove overlay | ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model / finance owners | Identify limitation; quantify adjustment | | Management | Approve rationale and amount | | Risk / validation | Challenge method and double-counting | | Audit committee / board where required | Oversee material judgement | | Assurance | Test evidence, controls and reporting | ### Permanent rule Every overlay needs a named residual risk, evidence, quantification method, owner and exit condition. ### Never confuse [Model recalibration] and [Post-model adjustment] **Model recalibration** — changes the model so it better reflects risk. --- **Post-model adjustment** — sits outside the model because a specific residual limitation remains. ### Permanent trap A permanent unexplained percentage added to ECL is not prudent judgement. It is an unvalidated parallel model. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) RBI’s Ind AS guidance for NBFCs requires governed, documented management overlays, including audit-committee approval. RBI’s bank ECL framework from 1 April 2027 also addresses model limitations and PMAs. #### UK (PRA) PRA thematic work in 2025 emphasised model boundaries, evolving risks, PMA governance and reducing adjustments as models improve. #### EU (EBA) EBA guidance requires sound governance; adjustments must remain consistent with unbiased accounting measurement. #### US (Federal Reserve / FDIC / OCC / NCUA) CECL allows judgement and qualitative adjustments, but the allowance process must be documented, supported and validated.

title: Validation, Backtesting and Staging Challenge
one_screen: Validation asks whether ECL is conceptually sound, correctly implemented and performing appropriately. Backtesting is one component; staging needs separate challenge because a good PD model can still produce late lifetime-loss recognition.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Validation layer | What is challenged | | :--- | :--- | | Conceptual soundness | Accounting objective and portfolio economics | | Data | Completeness, accuracy, representativeness | | Implementation | Code, transformations, mappings, aggregation | | PD | Discrimination, calibration, term structure, realised defaults | | LGD | Recovery amount, timing, costs, realised severity | | EAD | Drawdown, amortisation, exposure-at-default behaviour | | Staging | Migration timing, SICR triggers, rebuttals, cure | | Scenario / overlay | Sensitivity, weights, omitted risk, double-counting | | Governance | Approval, limitations, change control, challenge | ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Produces / challenges | | :--- | :--- | | Model owner | Model, data, documentation | | Independent validation | Conceptual and quantitative challenge | | Finance / credit risk | Use and interpretation | | Internal audit | Framework and control assurance | | Board / committees | Oversight of material models and findings | ### Permanent rule Validation tests the model against its intended use, not merely whether the developer’s calculation can be reproduced. ### Never confuse [Backtesting] and [Validation] **Backtesting** — compares predictions with realised outcomes. --- **Validation** — broader independent challenge of design, implementation, performance and use. ### Permanent trap A plausible aggregate allowance can hide offsetting PD, LGD, EAD or staging errors. “Total ECL looks reasonable” is not validation. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) RBI’s bank ECL framework from 1 April 2027 establishes model governance, independent validation and post-implementation backtesting. #### UK (PRA) PRA’s 2025 thematic feedback emphasises monitoring, validation and model operating boundaries. #### EU (EBA) EBA/GL/2017/06 sets expectations for sound ECL methodology and governance. #### US (Federal Reserve / FDIC / OCC / NCUA) Interagency guidance expects periodic validation independent of credit approval and allowance estimation, including conceptual soundness, monitoring and output analysis.

title: Allowance Movements and ECL Disclosures
one_screen: The closing allowance is not one opaque model output: it is the result of new business, repayments, stage migration, changed risk expectations, write-offs and other movements through the period. Disclosure makes those movements and the major judgements behind them observable.
bodyText: ### Formula ### Core mechanism | Movement | Typical allowance effect | | :--- | :--- | | New Stage 1 loan | Adds initial allowance | | Stage 1 → Stage 2 | Usually increases allowance horizon materially | | Stage 2 → Stage 1 | Usually releases part of allowance | | Stage 2 → Stage 3 | Remeasures lifetime loss under credit impairment | | Repayment / derecognition | Removes related allowance | | Better forecast / recovery | Can create impairment gain | | Write-off | Reduces gross asset and associated allowance | ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A movement in allowance should be explainable by changes in exposures, credit state, assumptions or recognised losses. ### Never confuse [Allowance reconciliation] and [Model validation] **Allowance reconciliation** — explains how the reported balance changed. --- **Model validation** — tests whether the process producing that balance is fit for purpose. ### Permanent trap A large unexplained “model change” or “management adjustment” line defeats the purpose of disclosure even if the arithmetic reconciliation balances. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Current commercial-bank IRACP has its own provisioning disclosures. RBI’s ECL framework from 1 April 2027 introduces stage-based ECL reporting and related disclosures. #### UK (UKEB) IFRS 7 requires explanations of credit-risk-management practices, ECL assumptions and loss-allowance movements. #### EU (European Commission / EBA) EU-adopted IFRS 7 and IFRS 9 apply; EBA supervision overlays the accounting disclosures. #### US (FASB) ASC 326 requires allowance, credit-quality, past-due and other relevant credit-loss disclosures rather than IFRS 9 stage reconciliations.

title: US CECL under ASC 326
one_screen: CECL is a forward-looking expected-loss model, but its architecture is not IFRS 9 staging. For in-scope financial assets measured at amortised cost, lifetime expected credit losses are generally recognised from initial recognition and re-estimated each reporting date.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Dimension | IFRS 9 general model | US CECL | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Initial allowance horizon | 12-month ECL | Lifetime expected loss | | SICR gateway | Yes | No | | Stage 1 / 2 / 3 | Yes | No equivalent allowance architecture | | Measurement methods | Method-neutral | Method-neutral | | Forward-looking information | Required | Historical experience + current conditions + reasonable and supportable forecasts | | Beyond supportable forecast | Framework remains probability-weighted and reasonable/supportable | Reversion to historical loss information | | Purchased impaired assets | POCI | PCD gross-up approach | ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule CECL’s absence of IFRS 9 staging does not mean credit deterioration is ignored. Deterioration changes a lifetime estimate that already exists. ### Never confuse [CECL lifetime allowance] and [IFRS 9 lifetime ECL] **CECL lifetime allowance** — generally recognised from initial recognition for in-scope amortised-cost assets. --- **IFRS 9 lifetime ECL** — generally begins after SICR, for credit-impaired assets, or where another IFRS 9 requirement specifies lifetime measurement. ### Permanent trap Creating IFRS 9-style stages inside CECL and using them to decide whether lifetime ECL applies imports a recognition threshold ASC 326 does not contain. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) CECL does not govern Indian statutory bank provisioning. Commercial banks currently use IRACP and move to RBI’s own staged ECL framework from 1 April 2027. #### UK (UKEB) UK-adopted IFRS 9 retains the 12-month / lifetime staging architecture. #### EU (European Commission) EU-adopted IFRS 9 retains staging. #### US (FASB) ASC 326 is the governing US GAAP credit-loss framework. It permits multiple estimation methods and separately addresses available-for-sale debt securities and off-balance-sheet exposures; unconditionally cancellable commitments do not receive an off-balance-sheet CECL allowance.

title: India: Parallel Regimes and the 2027 Bank ECL Transition
one_screen: India has parallel regimes. At 31 August 2026, banks remain under RBI IRACP through 31 March 2027; applicable NBFCs/ARCs use Ind AS with RBI safeguards; banks move to RBI’s staged-ECL framework on 1 April 2027.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Population / period | Regime | Recognition | Boundary | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Banks through 31 Mar 2027 | RBI IRACP 2025 | Classification + prescribed provisions | Not Ind AS 109 | | Applicable NBFCs / ARCs | Ind AS + RBI guidance | Ind AS 109 ECL + prudential comparison / impairment reserve | Accounting + prudential measures | | Banks from 1 Apr 2027 | RBI ECL Directions 2026 | Stage 1 12-month; Stage 2/3 lifetime ECL + floors | RBI, not Ind AS | | Same banks | Retained NPA rules | NPA classification beside staging | Stage 3 ≠ NPA | ### Flow ### Formula ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule RBI bank ECL is not bank adoption of Ind AS 109. ### Never confuse [Loss allowance] and [Capital] **Loss allowance** — measures expected credit loss and reduces carrying value or creates a provision. --- **Capital** — loss-absorbing resource. The CET1 add-back phases capital recognition of the transition; it does not turn ECL into capital. ### Never confuse [Stage 3] and [NPA] **Stage 3** — credit-impaired ECL state. --- **NPA** — classification under retained RBI rules. An exposure may satisfy both; they remain distinct. ### Permanent trap “Banks adopt Ind AS 109 on 1 April 2027” is wrong. Ind AS remains deferred; RBI’s 2026 Directions create a separate staged-ECL regime with floors and NPA classification. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) IRACP, Ind AS for applicable NBFCs/ARCs, and RBI bank ECL differ by entity and date. #### UK (UKEB) UK-adopted IFRS 9 has no equivalent transition. #### EU (European Commission) EU-adopted IFRS 9 does not use India’s entity split. #### US (FASB) US GAAP uses CECL, not RBI staged ECL.

title: RBI's Lending Mandate and Regulatory Perimeter
one_screen: RBI regulates Indian lending through a mix of prudential, conduct and developmental mandates. For a lender, the first question is not only "what risk rule applies?" but also "what type of regulated entity am I, what lending permissions do I have, and what directed-credit or customer-protection obligations attach to me?"
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Regulatory role | What it changes for lending | | :--- | :--- | | Prudential supervisor | Asset classification, provisioning, capital-related constraints, governance and supervisory expectations | | Conduct regulator | Pricing disclosure, fair practices, digital-lending controls, outsourcing and recovery conduct | | Developmental authority | Priority Sector Lending and inclusion-oriented credit architecture | | Licensing/perimeter authority | Which banks and non-banks may undertake lending and under what entity-specific rulebook | RBI's lending estate sits across the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, entity-specific Directions and subject-matter Directions. The same activity can therefore be governed by more than one instrument: a digital loan by an NBFC, for example, remains an NBFC exposure for prudential purposes while also falling under digital-lending conduct rules. This pack treats monetary policy only as an external input where a lending rule explicitly references it.
