Repo transmission, liquidity operations and balance-sheet liquidity are not re-taught here. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule The regulated entity remains responsible for the lending activity even when origination, servicing, data collection or recovery is outsourced. ### Permanent trap Treating an RBI circular as if it applied to every lender identically. Application usually depends on entity type, product and the specific Direction that governs that perimeter. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Banks Banking Regulation Act licensing and bank-specific Directions apply. #### NBFCs and HFCs RBI Act registration and entity-specific NBFC/HFC Directions apply, with additional layer-based deltas for NBFCs.

title: Indian Lending Entity Taxonomy
one_screen: India uses several regulated entity classes that look similar from a customer's perspective but have different lending permissions and supervisory treatment. The useful taxonomy is therefore functional: who may lend, who may accept deposits, and which RBI rulebook governs the exposure.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Entity class | Lending role | Key perimeter point | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Scheduled commercial banks | Full-service lending across retail, MSME and corporate segments | Bank prudential and conduct rules apply | | Small Finance Banks | Full-service banks with inclusion-oriented business constraints | Bank rules plus SFB-specific requirements | | Payments Banks | Payments and deposit services | They are not a general lending channel | | Regional Rural Banks | Rural and inclusion-focused banking | Separate statutory and RBI/NABARD-linked framework | | Cooperative banks | Member/community-oriented banking | Entity-specific cooperative-bank prudential treatment | | NBFCs | Non-bank lending and financial activity | RBI registration and NBFC Directions; SBR layer matters | | HFCs | Housing-finance-focused NBFC category | RBI-regulated and integrated into the NBFC prudential estate | | Account Aggregators | Consent-based financial-information intermediaries | They do not lend or hold the customer's financial information as their own asset | "Scheduled" is not a synonym for "commercial lender", and "NBFC" is not a small bank. The labels determine legal powers, funding model and applicable directions. ### Where it sits ### Never confuse [Payments Bank] and [Small Finance Bank] **Payments Bank** — a restricted bank focused on deposits and payments and not a general credit originator. --- **Small Finance Bank** — a bank that can lend and take deposits but operates with an inclusion-oriented mandate and specific business requirements. ### Permanent rule Before applying a lending rule, identify the regulated entity and the product. Similar customer journeys can sit on different legal and prudential estates. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Commercial banks, SFBs, RRBs and cooperative banks They are banks, but entity-specific prudential and PSL treatment differs. #### NBFCs and HFCs They are non-bank lenders; NBFC layer and activity type can change the governing requirements.

title: Bank versus NBFC: The Lending Boundary
one_screen: Banks and NBFCs can both make loans, but they are not interchangeable regulated objects. The decisive differences are banking powers, funding structure, access to the payment system and the prudential rulebook applied to the resulting credit exposure.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Dimension | Bank | NBFC | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Core legal status | Banking company or other bank category | Company undertaking regulated non-bank financial business | | Demand deposits | Banking power | Generally unavailable to NBFCs | | Payment-system role | Direct banking role, subject to applicable access rules | Not a substitute for a bank account/payment-system participant | | Funding | Customer deposits plus wholesale/market funding | Primarily borrowings, market funding and permitted deposits where authorised | | Prudential estate | Bank-specific capital, IRACP and conduct directions | NBFC-specific prudential directions, modified by activity and SBR layer | | Deposit protection | Bank deposits may fall within the statutory deposit-insurance framework | NBFC liabilities are not bank deposits merely because the entity lends | The practical consequence is that a loan with identical contractual cash flows can produce different regulatory obligations depending on whether it sits in a bank or NBFC. That affects governance, provisioning, reporting and sometimes customer-facing rules. One-line reminder: RWA and regulatory capital mechanics belong to CAP; this atom only identifies which Indian rulebook owns the exposure. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A non-bank lender does not become a bank because it performs bank-like credit underwriting or uses a bank-like digital interface. ### Permanent trap Applying a commercial-bank rule to an NBFC simply because both have the same borrower and product. The legal form of the lender determines the prudential starting point. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Scheduled commercial banks Full bank prudential estate applies. #### NBFCs Scale, activity and deposit-taking status determine additional prudential deltas.

title: NBFC Scale-Based Regulation
one_screen: Scale-Based Regulation, or SBR, makes "NBFC" only the starting label. RBI places NBFCs into Base, Middle, Upper and potentially Top layers so that regulatory intensity increases with size, activity, interconnectedness and systemic significance.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Layer | Regulatory idea | Lending consequence | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Base | Lowest-intensity layer for eligible smaller or specified NBFCs | Lighter prudential requirements than higher layers | | Middle | Larger, deposit-taking or specified important categories | Stronger governance and prudential requirements | | Upper | RBI-selected systemically significant NBFCs | Enhanced bank-like prudential and supervisory expectations | | Top | Exceptional supervisory layer | Additional restrictions can be imposed if systemic risk warrants | The architecture matters because the same NBFC activity can face different governance, exposure, provisioning or supervisory requirements after layer classification. RBI reorganised entity-wise NBFC instructions on 28 November 2025. The exact current post-consolidation instrument title and reference for every SBR provision is UNVERIFIED in this pack as at 31 August 2026; no unstated number is inferred from the superseded legacy text. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Layer is a regulatory attribute of the NBFC, not of an individual loan. ### Permanent trap Treating Base, Middle and Upper Layer as credit ratings. They classify regulatory intensity and systemic importance, not the probability that a particular borrower defaults. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Base Layer Lower-intensity requirements apply where the entity is eligible for Base Layer treatment. #### Middle and Upper Layer Additional prudential and governance obligations apply; Upper Layer placement reflects RBI's supervisory assessment.

title: Housing Finance Companies under RBI
one_screen: Housing Finance Companies are RBI-regulated non-bank lenders with a housing-finance business focus. The key teaching point is not the historical transfer from NHB itself, but the current position: HFCs sit inside RBI's NBFC regulatory estate while retaining HFC-specific business and prudential requirements.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Question | Current treatment | | :--- | :--- | | Who prudentially regulates HFCs? | RBI | | Are HFCs banks? | No; they are a distinct NBFC category | | Does SBR matter? | Yes; HFCs sit within the SBR architecture rather than outside it | | Do housing-specific conditions disappear? | No; HFC status carries activity-specific requirements | | What remains of NHB? | Policy, development and refinance functions continue, but HFC prudential supervision sits with RBI | The Finance Act changes made in 2019 transferred HFC regulatory authority to RBI. Subsequent RBI harmonisation brought HFC prudential treatment closer to other NBFCs while preserving housing-finance-specific eligibility and business rules. RBI reorganised entity-wise instructions on 28 November 2025 and amended parts of the HFC/NBFC estate in 2026. The exact current post-consolidation HFC instrument reference is UNVERIFIED here as at 31 August 2026. The pack therefore states the regulatory position without importing any legacy threshold or ratio that has not been established. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule An HFC is not outside NBFC regulation merely because its business is specialised housing finance. ### Never confuse [Housing Finance Company] and [National Housing Bank] **Housing Finance Company** — an RBI-regulated lender whose business is predominantly housing finance under the applicable definition. --- **National Housing Bank** — a housing-finance development and refinance institution; it is not the prudential supervisor replacing RBI for HFCs. ### Jurisdiction variants #### HFCs Housing-specific business tests and applicable prudential requirements apply. #### Other NBFCs General NBFC rules apply unless another activity-specific category modifies them.

title: Priority Sector Lending: Obligation and Applicability
one_screen: Priority Sector Lending, or PSL, converts RBI's developmental mandate into measurable lending obligations. It answers two questions before any category test begins: which lender is subject to PSL, and what overall target framework applies to that lender.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism PSL achievement is measured against the applicable RBI denominator, commonly expressed through Adjusted Net Bank Credit or the prescribed credit-equivalent base. PSL ratio = qualifying priority-sector credit / applicable PSL denominator | Entity | Overall architecture as at 31 August 2026 | | :--- | :--- | | Domestic commercial banks and qualifying foreign banks | Overall target plus prescribed sub-targets | | Small Finance Banks | Overall target of 60% under the 2025 Directions, plus applicable sub-targets | | Regional Rural Banks | Separate overall target of 75%, plus applicable sub-targets | | Urban cooperative banks and other covered entities | Entity-specific target structure under applicable Directions | | NBFCs | No general bank-style PSL target merely because they lend; their loans may matter through permitted on-lending or partnership structures | The 2025 Directions refreshed the PSL framework and were amended on 7 August 2026. A lender must therefore identify its own entity category before applying any target percentage. This atom owns target applicability only. Whether a particular agriculture, MSME, housing or other exposure qualifies is a separate eligibility question. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A loan contributes to PSL only when both conditions hold: the lender is measuring against an applicable PSL obligation and the exposure satisfies a qualifying category rule. ### Permanent trap Assuming one headline target applies to every bank. SFBs, RRBs, commercial banks and cooperative banks can have different target structures. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Small Finance Banks Overall PSL target is 60% under the 2025 Directions as at 31 August 2026. #### Regional Rural Banks A separate 75% overall target applies under the current framework. #### Other covered banks Apply the target and sub-target structure specified for that entity class.

title: Priority Sector Eligibility and Classification
one_screen: PSL is not a label a lender can attach to any socially useful loan. An exposure counts only when it satisfies the RBI definition for an eligible category, including borrower, purpose, size or activity conditions where the current Directions prescribe them.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Category family | Classification question | | :--- | :--- | | Agriculture | Is the borrower/activity within the permitted farm, allied, infrastructure or ancillary definitions? | | MSME | Does the enterprise meet the applicable MSME classification and is the credit eligible under PSL rules? | | Export credit | Is the exposure within the qualifying export-credit perimeter? | | Education | Does the loan satisfy the permitted education purpose and current conditions? | | Housing | Does the loan fit the qualifying housing purpose and applicable limits? | | Social infrastructure | Is the financed activity within the defined eligible infrastructure class? | | Renewable energy | Does the project or borrower fall within the prescribed renewable-energy category? | | Weaker sections | Does the borrower or exposure meet one of the specifically designated weaker-section conditions? | Classification is exposure-specific. A borrower can have one loan that qualifies and another that does not. The current Directions also distinguish direct lending, permitted on-lending and other structures, so the economic purpose alone is not enough. Every numerical eligibility threshold in the legacy pack is treated as unverified unless established from the current 2025 Directions as amended. This atom therefore teaches the classification logic without repeating stale rupee caps. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule PSL status follows the current RBI definition of the exposure, not the lender's internal product name or marketing label. ### Permanent trap Assuming "MSME borrower" automatically means every loan to that borrower is PSL. Purpose, product structure and current classification conditions still matter. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Commercial banks, SFBs and RRBs The same category definitions can feed different entity-specific target and sub-target structures. #### Cooperative banks Apply the category definitions together with the cooperative-bank PSL framework applicable to that entity.

title: PSL Achievement, PSLCs and Shortfalls
one_screen: A bank can meet PSL through qualifying assets on its own book and, where permitted, through the Priority Sector Lending Certificate market. PSLCs move regulatory achievement between banks without transferring the underlying loan, so credit risk and PSL compliance must be kept conceptually separate.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Object | What transfers? | What stays? | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Loan sale/assignment | Economic asset and agreed credit risk | Depends on transaction structure | | PSLC | PSL achievement for the specified certificate category | Underlying loan and borrower credit risk stay with originator | PSLCs exist in category forms aligned to the RBI framework. They allow a bank that is short in one target or sub-target to buy achievement from another institution that has excess qualifying lending. Where an institution still has a shortfall after permitted adjustments, the RBI framework can require contribution or placement into specified development or financial-inclusion arrangements. Exact current shortfall mechanics depend on entity and the 2025 Directions as amended. ### Where it sits ### Never confuse [PSLC] and [Loan sale] **PSLC** — a regulatory certificate transferring PSL achievement. --- **Loan sale** — a transaction transferring an economic loan asset or interest in it. ### Permanent rule Buying a PSLC does not make the buyer the creditor of the underlying borrower. ### Permanent trap Using PSLC purchases as evidence that the buyer has acquired the corresponding credit exposure. The regulatory achievement moves; the loan does not. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Banks eligible for PSLC participation Certificate use follows the current RBI PSL framework and the category of shortfall. #### Entities outside the PSLC framework No certificate treatment should be inferred merely because the entity makes priority-sector-like loans.

title: Fair Lending: KFS, APR, Charges and Disclosure
one_screen: Indian lending conduct rules increasingly force price and key contractual terms into a standard pre-contract disclosure. The Key Facts Statement, or KFS, is the central customer-facing object: it makes the annual percentage rate and material charges visible before the borrower is bound.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Item | Conduct purpose | | :--- | :--- | | Interest rate | Shows the contractual borrowing rate | | APR | Captures the all-in annualised cost using the prescribed methodology | | Fees and charges | Prevents undisclosed price components | | Penal charges | Separates a contractual penalty from disguised compounding of interest | | Repayment schedule | Makes timing and total repayment obligations legible | | Grievance contact | Gives the borrower a route to challenge conduct or servicing | KFS requirements apply across specified retail and MSME lending contexts and are also built into digital-lending controls. This atom owns the disclosure object itself; a digital channel does not create a separate economics standard. RBI reorganised responsible-business-conduct instructions in 2025. The exact cross-entity post-consolidation reference set is UNVERIFIED here as at 31 August 2026, so no unestablished coverage threshold is stated. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A fee that forms part of the borrower's cost cannot be made compliant by hiding it outside the stated interest rate. ### Never confuse [Interest rate] and [APR] **Interest rate** — the contractual rate charged on the loan balance. --- **APR** — the prescribed annualised measure of total borrowing cost, including covered charges. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Banks and covered NBFCs KFS and fair-practice requirements apply through the relevant RBI conduct Directions. #### Digital lending The same disclosure principle is reinforced through digital-lending-specific delivery and consent requirements.

title: Lending Rates: Benchmark, Spread, Reset and Prepayment
one_screen: RBI does not prescribe one universal lending-rate formula for every Indian loan. Rate governance depends on lender and product, but the recurring structure is benchmark plus contractual spread, with rules on reset, borrower communication and, for specified floating-rate loans, prepayment treatment.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Loan rate = benchmark + contractual spread Benchmark = the reference rate specified by the applicable RBI framework or lender methodology. Spread = borrower/product margin added to the benchmark under the lender's approved pricing policy. | Question | Regulatory control | | :--- | :--- | | What benchmark is permitted? | Depends on entity and product | | Can spread change arbitrarily? | No; changes must follow the permitted contractual and policy framework | | What happens at reset? | Rate or instalment/tenor implications must be handled under applicable borrower-protection rules | | Can prepayment attract charges? | Treatment depends on loan type, borrower class and current RBI directions | A draft Reserve Bank of India (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026 consultation was issued in August 2026. As at 31 August 2026 it is a proposal, not a rule in force. This atom therefore teaches the extant entity/product framework and does not treat the consultation text as implemented law. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A floating-rate loan must follow the benchmark/reset mechanics that govern that product; "floating" does not mean the lender may reprice without a defined rule. ### Permanent trap Teaching the August 2026 consultation as already effective. Its proposed consolidation is future-facing as at 31 August 2026. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Scheduled commercial banks External-benchmark or other bank-specific benchmark requirements apply by product class. #### NBFCs and HFCs Pricing remains subject to their fair-practice and board-approved pricing framework; bank benchmark rules should not be imported automatically.

title: Digital Lending Perimeter: RE, LSP and DLA
one_screen: Digital lending changes the channel, not the identity of the regulated creditor. RBI separates the Regulated Entity that owns the loan, the Lending Service Provider that performs outsourced functions, and the Digital Lending App through which the customer may interact.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Role | What it does | What it does not become | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Regulated Entity (RE) | Sanctions, funds or owns the regulated credit exposure | It does not shed responsibility by outsourcing | | Lending Service Provider (LSP) | Performs one or more customer acquisition, underwriting-support, servicing or recovery functions under contract | It is not automatically the lender | | Digital Lending App (DLA) | Customer-facing digital interface operated by or for an RE/LSP | The app itself is not the regulatory creditor | The legal and prudential loan remains with the RE. RBI therefore focuses heavily on outsourcing accountability, disclosure of the RE, permitted data collection and customer treatment. An LSP can influence underwriting or servicing operationally, but the RE must perform due diligence on the LSP and remains responsible for compliance. A technology layer cannot be used to create an unregulated pass-through lender. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule The regulated lender remains responsible for acts performed through its LSP or DLA within the lending arrangement. ### Never confuse [LSP] and [Lender] **LSP** — a service provider acting for a regulated lender under a contractual arrangement. --- **Lender** — the regulated entity that owns or extends the credit under the applicable RBI perimeter. ### Permanent trap Assuming a fintech brand shown to the customer is necessarily the balance-sheet lender. The underlying RE must be identified. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Banks and NBFCs Both can use LSPs and DLAs, but their underlying prudential treatment remains entity-specific. #### Non-regulated technology firms They may act as service providers where permitted, but they do not obtain lending powers merely by operating an app.

title: Digital Lending Transaction and Customer Controls
one_screen: RBI's digital-lending rules control the customer journey as well as the lender's legal perimeter. The core idea is traceability: the borrower should know the regulated lender, understand the price, consent to data use, and have funds and repayments move through permitted channels.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Control | Why it exists | | :--- | :--- | | KFS and offer disclosure | Prevents hidden pricing and lender ambiguity | | Explicit consent | Restricts unnecessary or covert data access | | Need-based data collection | Limits data extraction unrelated to lending | | Direct disbursal/repayment | Reduces uncontrolled pass-through handling by LSPs | | Cooling-off or look-up period where applicable | Gives the borrower a defined exit route | | Grievance officer and escalation | Keeps digital delivery inside normal accountability | Permitted exceptions to direct fund flow exist only where the Directions expressly allow them. The operational default is not "money may pass through the fintech because the fintech sourced the customer." ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Digital convenience does not displace borrower consent, price transparency or the regulated entity's responsibility. ### Permanent trap Treating an LSP collection account as the natural centre of the transaction. RBI's design generally keeps loan disbursal and repayment tied directly to the regulated lender and borrower, subject only to specified exceptions. ### Jurisdiction variants No within-India delta in the core digital control logic; entity-specific prudential treatment continues underneath the digital channel.

title: Default Loss Guarantee
one_screen: RBI's current term is Default Loss Guarantee, or DLG. A DLG is credit support provided to a regulated lender against losses on a fixed, identifiable loan portfolio; it does not turn the guarantor into the lender and it does not delay NPA recognition.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism DLG cap = 5% of amount disbursed out of the fixed DLG set DLG set = the identifiable portfolio specified upfront for the guarantee arrangement. Amount disbursed = the amount actually disbursed from that fixed portfolio at the relevant point under the Direction. | DLG does | DLG does not | | :--- | :--- | | Provides contractual first-loss-style credit support | Replace underwriting | | Reduces the lender's realised loss when validly invoked | Change the borrower into a non-defaulting borrower | | Operates against a fixed identifiable portfolio | Apply a separate Rs 5 crore ceiling | | Is subject to eligibility, form and disclosure conditions | Make NPA recognition disappear | The legacy expression "FLDG / First Loss Default Guarantee" is not used here because RBI's current Directions use DLG. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule DLG support and borrower asset classification are separate. A guaranteed default can still be an NPA. ### Never confuse [DLG] and [Securitisation] **DLG** — contractual loss support on a fixed loan portfolio. --- **Securitisation** — transfer of credit exposures into a structured asset-transfer framework governed by separate RBI rules. ### Jurisdiction variants No within-India delta in the core DLG cap basis under the Digital Lending Directions; eligibility and prudential effects still depend on the participating regulated entity.

title: Co-Lending Arrangements: Structure and Risk Retention
one_screen: RBI's 2025 Co-Lending Arrangements Directions govern joint lending by eligible regulated entities to a common borrower. The defining idea is genuine shared exposure: each participating RE must hold an agreed portion of every loan and retain at least the prescribed minimum share.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Feature | Current rule architecture | | :--- | :--- | | Minimum retention | Each participating RE retains at least 10% of each individual loan | | Effective date | Directions apply from 1 January 2026 | | Loan ownership | Each RE owns and records its share | | Customer terms | Agreement must make the co-lending structure and roles transparent | | Risk | Credit loss follows each RE's exposure, subject to any separately permitted support arrangement | This replaces the older shorthand that co-lending meant an 80:20 bank/NBFC structure. An 80:20 commercial split can still occur contractually, but it is not the current universal regulatory formula. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Co-lending is not a disguised loan from one RE to another; each participating RE must hold a real share of the end-borrower exposure. ### Never confuse [Co-lending] and [Syndication] **Co-lending** — a regulated joint-lending arrangement governed by RBI's co-lending Directions. --- **Syndication** — a broader multi-lender financing structure that is not defined by the specific co-lending framework. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Participating banks and NBFCs Each applies its own prudential rules to its retained share while complying with the common co-lending framework.

title: Co-Lending Operations and Classification Synchronisation
one_screen: The hardest part of co-lending is operational consistency across two regulated balance sheets. Each RE books only its share, but the borrower experience, servicing data, credit-information reporting and stress classification must be coordinated so that one common loan does not become two contradictory regulatory stories.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Operating object | Required discipline | | :--- | :--- | | Disbursement | Each RE's funded share must be traceable | | Servicing | Roles, collection channels and borrower communication are contractually defined | | Cash allocation | Principal, interest and charges are split under the agreed mechanism | | Reconciliation | Both REs reconcile balances, ageing and collections | | CIC reporting | Each RE reports its share consistently with the arrangement | | Stress status | Required SMA/NPA information is exchanged so classification is synchronised where the Directions require it | One-line reminder: IRACP determines Indian prudential stress status; ECL staging remains an IMP concept. The 2025 co-lending framework specifically addresses borrower-level information sharing and alignment. That does not mean the two REs necessarily hold identical provisions, because provisioning can depend on each entity's applicable prudential rulebook. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Operational servicing may be centralised, but regulatory ownership remains divided according to each RE's retained exposure. ### Never confuse [Classification synchronisation] and [Identical provisioning] **Classification synchronisation** — aligned recognition of borrower stress or NPA status where required. --- **Identical provisioning** — the same provision percentage on both books; this does not automatically follow because entity-specific prudential rules can differ. ### Permanent trap Booking the entire co-lent exposure in one RE and treating the other RE as only a funding provider. That defeats the borrower-level risk-sharing structure. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Bank participant Applies bank prudential rules to its share. #### NBFC participant Applies the applicable NBFC prudential rules to its share, including any layer-based delta.

title: Account Aggregator Consent Architecture
one_screen: The Account Aggregator, or AA, framework lets a customer move financial information between regulated participants through a standard consent architecture. The AA is neither the lender nor the data owner: it manages permissioned transmission between a Financial Information Provider and a Financial Information User.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Role | Lending relevance | | :--- | :--- | | Customer | Controls consent | | Financial Information Provider (FIP) | Holds source financial information | | Account Aggregator | Consent and transmission intermediary | | Financial Information User (FIU) | Receives information for a permitted purpose, such as underwriting | Consent defines scope, purpose, data type and duration under the applicable framework. The AA is designed to avoid uncontrolled credential sharing and manual statement exchange. One-line reminder: BCBS 239 and enterprise data governance belong to DAT; this atom owns the Indian consent rail. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule The AA cannot convert customer consent for one defined purpose into unrestricted future access to the customer's financial information. ### Never confuse [Account Aggregator] and [Credit Bureau] **Account Aggregator** — transmits customer-permissioned financial information for a defined consented purpose. --- **Credit Bureau** — stores and reports credit-information history under the Credit Information Companies framework. ### Permanent trap Treating AA consent as a lender's right to scrape any available financial data. The consent artefact is scoped and purpose-bound. ### Jurisdiction variants No within-India delta in the core AA role; participation obligations differ by whether an entity is acting as FIP, FIU or AA.

title: Lending Data Rails: GSTN, ULI and the OCEN Boundary
one_screen: India's lending stack increasingly separates data access from credit decisioning. GST and other public or financial data can feed underwriting through consented or authorised rails, while the Unified Lending Interface, or ULI, standardises access to multiple data sources; OCEN is best treated as adjacent open credit-enablement infrastructure, not as an RBI-regulated lender.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Component | Role in lending | | :--- | :--- | | GSTN and other source systems | Originate verified business or public-sector data | | AA ecosystem | Carries consented financial information | | ULI | Provides a standardised interface for lenders to access permitted data sources | | OCEN | Open protocol approach for connecting borrower-facing platforms and lenders | | Bank/NBFC | Performs underwriting, sanctions credit and owns the loan | ULI and OCEN do not remove the need for a regulated lender, KFS, underwriting governance or customer consent. They reduce friction in data collection and offer distribution. The precise 2026 production status and instrument reference for every ULI/OCEN component is not established in this pack as at 31 August 2026. No unverified rollout statistic or mandatory-adoption claim is stated. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A data rail can accelerate lending, but it does not itself sanction credit or absorb borrower default risk. ### Never confuse [ULI] and [Lender] **ULI** — infrastructure for standardised access to permitted lending data. --- **Lender** — the regulated entity that decides, contracts and owns the credit exposure. ### Jurisdiction variants No within-India delta in the infrastructure concept; actual participation depends on each entity's technical and regulatory eligibility.

title: Credit Information Ecosystem: CIC, CIR and Bureau Score
one_screen: India's Credit Information Companies, or CICs, collect regulated credit information from lenders and return Credit Information Reports and related scores. A bureau score is a proprietary risk signal derived from reported history; it is not an RBI approval threshold and it does not replace underwriting.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Object | What it contains or represents | | :--- | :--- | | Credit Information Report (CIR) | Detailed reported credit accounts, balances, enquiries and repayment/default history | | Bureau score | Model-generated summary signal based on bureau data | | Lender credit decision | Broader assessment using bureau data plus income, cash flow, collateral, policy and other evidence | RBI regulates the reporting relationship between credit institutions and CICs, including data quality, update and customer correction expectations. A high score is not a guarantee of repayment; a low or missing score is not by itself a regulatory prohibition on lending. One-line reminder: model validation belongs to MRM. This atom owns what the bureau object is, not how its proprietary model is validated. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Credit information is an input to a lender's decision, not a substitute for the lender's own credit assessment. ### Never confuse [Credit Information Report] and [Credit score] **Credit Information Report** — the detailed borrower-level reported credit history. --- **Credit score** — a model-generated summary indicator derived from bureau information. ### Jurisdiction variants No material within-India delta in the concept; different CICs may use different proprietary score methodologies.

title: Credit Information Reporting and Correction Cycle
one_screen: Credit-information regulation is operational: lenders must submit accurate borrower data, CICs must process it, and customers need a route to challenge errors. The value of the bureau system depends on update discipline because stale arrears, closed loans or incorrect balances can distort subsequent lending decisions.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Control point | Failure it prevents | | :--- | :--- | | Regular reporting | Missing or stale credit history | | Standard data fields | Inconsistent borrower/account interpretation | | Data-quality checks | Wrong balances, status or identifiers | | Dispute workflow | Persistent customer harm from erroneous reporting | | Closure/update process | Accounts remaining incorrectly shown as active or delinquent | RBI strengthened credit-information reporting and customer compensation/correction expectations through recent directions. Further amendments took effect during the 2025-2026 period. The exact post-consolidation amendment references are UNVERIFIED in this pack as at 31 August 2026, so no unsupported reporting-frequency number is stated here. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A lender's obligation is not satisfied by submitting data once; reported credit information must remain accurate as the account changes. ### Permanent trap Treating a bureau error as solely the CIC's problem. The originating credit institution is responsible for the accuracy of the data it supplies and must participate in correction. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Banks and NBFCs that are credit institutions Reporting obligations apply through the CIC framework. #### CICs They have separate duties for record handling, dispute management and customer access.

title: IRACP: India's Prudential Asset-Quality Regime
one_screen: IRACP is India's prudential regime for Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning on advances. It answers whether a loan is performing or non-performing for RBI purposes, what income may be recognised and what minimum prudential provision is required; it is distinct from Ind AS 109 ECL.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | IRACP object | Question answered | | :--- | :--- | | SMA | Is the exposure showing pre-NPA repayment stress? | | NPA recognition | Has the prudential non-performing trigger been met? | | Asset class | How seasoned or impaired is the NPA for prudential purposes? | | Income recognition | Can accrued income still be recognised? | | Provision | What minimum prudential loss buffer is required? | RBI reorganised entity-wise prudential instructions on 28 November 2025. As at 31 August 2026 commercial banks remain on the current IRACP framework, while RBI has already issued a future ECL-based prudential framework scheduled to begin on 1 April 2027. That future framework is not treated as current law in this pack. The exact post-consolidation reference for every bank/NBFC/HFC IRACP provision is UNVERIFIED where not separately stated. ### Where it sits ### Never confuse [IRACP] and [Ind AS 109 ECL] **IRACP** — RBI prudential classification, income-recognition and minimum-provisioning regime. --- **Ind AS 109 ECL** — accounting impairment methodology owned by IMP. ### Permanent rule IRACP status does not disappear because an accounting ECL model produces a different loss estimate. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Commercial banks Current 2025 entity-wise IRACP Directions apply as at 31 August 2026, with prudential ECL transition scheduled for 1 April 2027. #### NBFCs and HFCs Apply their current entity-wise prudential Directions; exact post-consolidation references are UNVERIFIED here.

title: Special Mention Accounts
one_screen: Special Mention Accounts, or SMAs, are RBI's pre-NPA stress buckets for specified credit exposures. They create a disciplined early-warning ladder before the standard 90-day NPA threshold, and the legacy pack's 31-60, 61-90 and 91-180 day sequence is incorrect.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism For term loans, the corrected delinquency sequence is: | Status | Days past due | | :--- | :--- | | SMA-0 | Up to 30 days | | SMA-1 | More than 30 days and up to 60 days | | SMA-2 | More than 60 days and up to 90 days | | NPA | More than 90 days, subject to the applicable prudential rule | The account's overdue status is determined from the contractual due date and day-end process under the applicable Directions. Other products, especially revolving facilities such as cash credit or overdraft, can use "out of order" or other product-specific tests rather than a simple instalment count. SMA is a stress-monitoring classification; it is not the same object as Stage 2 under Ind AS 109. ### Where it sits ### Never confuse [SMA-2] and [NPA] **SMA-2** — the final pre-NPA delinquency bucket for the applicable exposure. --- **NPA** — prudential non-performing status once the relevant RBI trigger is crossed. ### Permanent rule SMA categories are not optional watchlist labels; where the framework applies, they follow the prescribed repayment-status logic. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Term loans Days-past-due buckets drive SMA status. #### Cash credit and overdraft facilities Product-specific "out of order" logic applies alongside the broader prudential framework.

title: NPA Recognition, Income Recognition and Asset Classes
one_screen: An NPA is a prudential status, not merely an internal "bad loan" label. Once the applicable RBI trigger is met, income recognition changes and the exposure moves through sub-standard, doubtful and loss categories according to the current entity-specific IRACP rules.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Step | Prudential effect | | :--- | :--- | | NPA trigger reached | Exposure becomes non-performing under the applicable rule | | Income recognition restriction | Unrealised interest cannot continue to be treated like normal performing income | | Sub-standard | Initial NPA class under the prudential seasoning framework | | Doubtful | NPA remains unresolved beyond the prescribed period | | Loss | Asset is identified as uncollectible or of such little value that full recognition of loss is required | For many term-loan exposures, the familiar trigger is more than 90 days overdue. Product-specific rules matter: cash credit/overdraft facilities use "out of order" criteria, and certain agricultural or other specialised exposures can follow different tests. RBI also applies borrower/account-level disciplines intended to prevent selective treatment of one facility while another exposure to the same borrower is non-performing, subject to the applicable Direction. Exact seasoning periods and special-product rules in the post-28 November 2025 entity-wise Directions are not restated here unless established; any unresolved reference is treated as UNVERIFIED as at 31 August 2026. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Once an exposure is NPA, income recognition cannot continue as though contractual accrual automatically equals realised income. ### Never confuse [NPA status] and [Write-off] **NPA status** — prudential classification of a live credit exposure. --- **Write-off** — accounting removal of some or all of an exposure; legal recovery rights can continue. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Term lending More-than-90-days overdue is the core trigger for ordinary term-loan treatment. #### Revolving and specialised facilities Apply the product-specific "out of order" or other prescribed test.

title: RBI Regulatory Provisioning
one_screen: RBI prudential provisioning attaches a minimum loss buffer to an exposure's regulatory classification and security position. The provision is not the same object as an accounting ECL allowance, even where both respond to the same borrower deterioration.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Prudential input | Effect on required provision | | :--- | :--- | | Standard versus NPA status | NPA generally attracts higher minimum provisioning | | Sub-standard/doubtful/loss class | More severe or seasoned classes attract stronger provisioning | | Secured versus unsecured portion | Realisable security can affect the applicable minimum | | Time spent in doubtful status | Seasoning can increase the required provision | | Entity type | Banks, NBFCs, HFCs and cooperative banks can sit on different schedules | The applicable provisioning percentages sit in the current entity-wise RBI Directions. The exact post-consolidation reference and full percentage schedule for every entity are not established here as at 31 August 2026. They remain UNVERIFIED rather than being copied from the legacy pack. That means this atom teaches the invariant mechanism without inventing a number: classification, security and seasoning determine the prudential floor. A lender may hold a higher provision under internal policy or accounting rules. One-line reminder: ECL measurement and staging belong to IMP. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule RBI prudential provisions are minimum regulatory requirements; a lower accounting estimate does not automatically eliminate the prudential floor. ### Never confuse [Prudential provision] and [ECL allowance] **Prudential provision** — RBI-prescribed minimum buffer linked to the prudential classification framework. --- **ECL allowance** — accounting impairment measured under Ind AS 109 for entities to which it applies. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Commercial banks Apply the bank provisioning schedule in the current entity-wise IRACP Directions. #### NBFCs and HFCs Apply the applicable entity-wise prudential schedule; exact post-consolidation references and percentages are UNVERIFIED here as at 31 August 2026.

title: IRACP versus Ind AS 109: Parallel Regimes and Prudential Floor
one_screen: For Ind AS-applicable NBFCs and HFCs, accounting impairment and RBI prudential asset-quality rules run in parallel. Ind AS 109 determines the accounting ECL allowance; RBI IRACP still determines prudential classification and the minimum regulatory requirement, with a prescribed treatment when the prudential amount is higher.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism One-line reminder: Ind AS 109 uses forward-looking ECL and staging; those mechanics belong to IMP. | Object | Owner | Purpose | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | ECL allowance | Ind AS 109 | Accounting impairment | | IRACP classification | RBI | Prudential asset-quality status | | Prudential minimum | RBI | Regulatory loss buffer | | Impairment reserve / prudential shortfall treatment | RBI framework for Ind AS entities | Prevents accounting ECL below the prudential floor from weakening regulatory protection | The exact post-consolidation entity-wise wording and reserve mechanics are UNVERIFIED here as at 31 August 2026 where not separately established. No percentage or formula is inferred. Commercial banks are in a separate transition: as at 31 August 2026 the current IRACP framework remains in force, with an RBI prudential ECL framework scheduled for 1 April 2027. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Accounting ECL does not replace RBI prudential classification for entities that must comply with both regimes. ### Never confuse [Ind AS 109 staging] and [SMA/NPA] **Ind AS 109 staging** — accounting impairment status based on credit deterioration and default concepts. --- **SMA/NPA** — RBI prudential repayment-stress and non-performing classifications. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Ind AS-applicable NBFCs and HFCs Run accounting ECL and RBI prudential requirements in parallel. #### Commercial banks Current IRACP remains in force on 31 August 2026; prudential ECL transition begins 1 April 2027.

title: NPA Cure and Upgrade
one_screen: Upgrade reverses prudential NPA status only when the RBI cure conditions are actually met. The core distinction is between curing ordinary arrears by clearing overdue amounts and demonstrating satisfactory performance after a restructuring, where additional monitoring conditions can apply.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Situation | Upgrade logic | | :--- | :--- | | Ordinary arrears-driven NPA | Borrower must clear the amounts required by the current prudential rule so the account is no longer overdue in the prescribed manner | | Multiple facilities to same borrower | Borrower-level treatment can require all relevant arrears to be regularised before upgrade | | Restructured exposure | Upgrade depends on the post-restructuring performance conditions in the applicable resolution framework | | Technical write-off | Does not itself cure borrower default or restore standard status | The legacy pack's generic "two quarters or one year" cure rule is not carried forward. The correct performance period depends on the applicable current framework and exposure type. RBI's 28 November 2025 consolidation reorganised the prudential directions. Exact post-consolidation upgrade wording for every entity and restructured exposure is UNVERIFIED here as at 31 August 2026; no unsupported period is stated. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A payment that reduces arrears is not automatically enough for upgrade; the account must satisfy the full applicable RBI cure condition. ### Never confuse [Cure] and [Restructuring] **Cure** — borrower performance removes the prudential default condition. --- **Restructuring** — contractual terms are modified because of borrower financial difficulty or resolution needs; separate upgrade conditions can follow. ### Permanent trap Upgrading an account immediately because one overdue instalment was paid. The test is whether the account as a whole has been regularised under the applicable rule. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Ordinary bank/NBFC exposures Apply the current entity-wise cure and borrower-level rules. #### Restructured exposures Apply the additional performance conditions in the relevant resolution framework.

title: Resolution and Restructuring of Stressed Assets
one_screen: RBI's stressed-asset resolution framework governs what lenders may do when borrower stress requires more than ordinary collection. Resolution can include restructuring, change in ownership, additional finance or other agreed measures, but it must be a governed response to financial stress rather than a device for concealing default.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Resolution tool | Core purpose | | :--- | :--- | | Restructuring | Modify contractual terms to make viable repayment possible | | Change in ownership/control | Replace an unsustainable ownership structure where permitted | | Additional finance | Support an implementable resolution rather than simply capitalise old arrears | | Inter-creditor coordination | Align multiple lenders on a common plan | | Exit/enforcement | Used when consensual resolution is not viable | Historical schemes such as CDR, 5/25 and pandemic-era dispensations are not taught as current parallel regimes. They matter only as historical context for why RBI moved toward a more general resolution framework. RBI consolidated entity-wise instructions in 2025. The exact current post-consolidation reference and any exposure-specific implementation period not established here remain UNVERIFIED as at 31 August 2026. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Restructuring changes contractual terms; it does not automatically erase the prudential consequences of borrower stress. ### Never confuse [Resolution] and [Evergreening] **Resolution** — a governed plan intended to restore sustainable repayment or realise value. --- **Evergreening** — new or modified credit used mainly to conceal an existing default without genuine resolution. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Single-lender exposures Resolution can be implemented within the lender's own governance subject to RBI rules. #### Multi-lender exposures Inter-creditor coordination and common implementation requirements become central.

title: Compromise Settlements and Technical Write-Offs
one_screen: Compromise settlement and technical write-off are different exit tools. A compromise changes the amount or terms the creditor agrees to accept in full or partial settlement; a technical write-off removes an exposure from the active books while legal recovery rights can continue.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Tool | What changes | What can remain | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Compromise settlement | Contractual recovery outcome is agreed for less than or differently from the original dues | Governance, sacrifice recognition and any cooling-off conditions | | Technical write-off | Accounting carrying amount is removed after applicable provisioning/write-off process | Legal claim and recovery action may continue | | Waiver/forgiveness | Creditor intentionally gives up part of the legal claim | Only the residual claim, if any | | Recovery after write-off | Cash is collected after accounting removal | Legal enforcement remains possible if claim survives | RBI's 2023 framework formalised governance for compromise settlements and technical write-offs, including board-approved policies, delegation and treatment of fraud or wilful-default cases under the applicable conditions. A write-off is therefore not evidence that the borrower was "forgiven". Nor does a compromise erase the need to record the economic sacrifice and follow applicable credit-information and re-lending rules. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Technical write-off changes accounting presentation, not automatically the borrower's legal liability. ### Never confuse [Technical write-off] and [Debt waiver] **Technical write-off** — accounting removal while recovery can continue. --- **Debt waiver** — creditor relinquishment of the legal claim to the waived amount. ### Permanent trap Telling a borrower or stakeholder that "written off" means "no longer owed". That conclusion depends on the legal settlement, not the accounting entry. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Banks and NBFCs Both apply the RBI governance framework subject to their entity-specific policy and prudential treatment.

title: SARFAESI and DRT: Secured Enforcement and Tribunal Route
one_screen: SARFAESI gives eligible secured creditors a statutory route to enforce qualifying security interests without first obtaining an ordinary civil-court decree, while Debt Recovery Tribunals provide a specialised adjudicatory and recovery forum. The two are connected but not interchangeable: SARFAESI is an enforcement power; DRT is a tribunal route.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Route | Core object | | :--- | :--- | | SARFAESI | Enforcement of qualifying security interest by an eligible secured creditor | | DRT | Specialised recovery/adjudication forum under the debt-recovery statute | | DRAT | Appellate forum for DRT decisions | | ARC involvement | Acquisition/reconstruction and enforcement of stressed financial assets under the statutory framework | SARFAESI does not turn an unsecured personal loan into a secured claim. Eligibility, excluded security types and monetary/forum thresholds are statutory and can change; no legacy threshold is repeated here unless established. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule SARFAESI power depends on a qualifying secured interest and statutory eligibility; default alone is not enough. ### Never confuse [SARFAESI] and [DRT] **SARFAESI** — statutory secured-creditor enforcement mechanism. --- **DRT** — tribunal that hears recovery applications and challenges within its jurisdiction. ### Permanent trap Using SARFAESI as shorthand for all Indian debt collection. Unsecured claims and other recovery routes sit outside that secured-enforcement mechanism. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Eligible secured creditors May use SARFAESI where statutory conditions are met. #### Unsecured or otherwise excluded claims Must rely on other contractual, tribunal, insolvency or court routes as applicable.

title: IBC: Collective Insolvency and Competing Enforcement
one_screen: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, or IBC, shifts a stressed corporate borrower from individual creditor enforcement into a collective insolvency process once the statutory process is admitted. The central lending insight is the moratorium: after admission, creditors cannot continue separate enforcement as though the insolvency case did not exist.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | IBC object | Lending consequence | | :--- | :--- | | Admission | Starts the formal collective process | | Moratorium | Stays specified individual enforcement and recovery actions | | Committee of Creditors | Financial creditors exercise collective decision rights | | Resolution plan | Can restructure debt, ownership and recoveries | | Liquidation | Value is realised under the statutory waterfall if resolution fails | The legacy pack's voting percentages, default threshold and timetable figures are not carried forward here because they were specifically treated as unverified. The Code and amendments govern those details; this atom preserves the mechanism without guessing numbers. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Once the insolvency proceeding is admitted and the moratorium applies, individual enforcement routes cannot simply continue unaffected. ### Never confuse [IBC filing] and [IBC admission] **IBC filing** — an application has been submitted. --- **IBC admission** — the adjudicating authority has admitted the case, triggering the statutory insolvency process and moratorium consequences. ### Permanent trap Assuming a creditor vote is required before any financial creditor can file an application. Filing rights and later committee voting are separate statutory questions. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Corporate persons Corporate insolvency runs through the National Company Law Tribunal architecture. #### Individuals and other debtor categories Different insolvency/recovery provisions and forums can apply; this atom does not import the corporate process automatically.

title: Recovery Conduct, Recovery Agents and Escalation
one_screen: Indian lenders remain responsible for how overdue debt is collected, including conduct by outsourced recovery agents. Recovery rights do not authorise intimidation, public shaming, misleading representations or uncontrolled contact; borrower grievance and RBI ombudsman routes remain available even when the account is genuinely in default.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Recovery control | Required outcome | | :--- | :--- | | Agent due diligence and authorisation | Lender knows who acts on its behalf | | Identity and communication discipline | Borrower can identify the lender/agent and reason for contact | | Contact controls | Recovery activity occurs within permitted conduct boundaries | | No harassment or intimidation | Default does not remove dignity and fair-treatment obligations | | Complaint handling | Borrower can escalate misconduct to the regulated entity | | Ombudsman route | Eligible unresolved service grievances can move to RBI's external redress framework | The lender cannot outsource accountability. If an agent breaches conduct rules, the regulated entity faces supervisory and customer-redress consequences. RBI issued recovery-conduct amendments on 6 August 2026 with an effective date of 1 January 2027. As at 31 August 2026 those future-effective provisions are not yet in force. This atom therefore distinguishes the current conduct framework from the 2027 amendments and does not backdate future requirements. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A valid debt does not legalise abusive collection. The lender is accountable for outsourced recovery conduct. ### Never confuse [Recovery right] and [Recovery method] **Recovery right** — the creditor's lawful claim to collect or enforce the debt. --- **Recovery method** — the manner in which collection is carried out; it remains subject to RBI conduct rules. ### Permanent trap Treating a third-party recovery agent as outside the lender's compliance perimeter. Outsourcing the call or visit does not outsource regulatory responsibility. ### Jurisdiction variants #### Banks, NBFCs and other covered REs Apply the conduct and outsourcing requirements relevant to their entity class. #### Future position from 1 January 2027 RBI's 6 August 2026 recovery-conduct amendments become effective; they are future rules as at 31 August 2026 and are not treated as currently operative.

title: What Counts as a Model
one_screen: A model is a governed representation that transforms inputs into outputs using assumptions and quantitative or cognitive techniques. Classification is consequential: model status brings inventory, validation, approval, monitoring and change controls, while the legal boundary differs materially across jurisdictions.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Test | Question | | :--- | :--- | | Inputs | Does it consume data, estimates, judgement or structured inputs? | | Transformation | Does it apply statistical, mathematical, economic, financial or comparable analytical assumptions or techniques? | | Output | Does it estimate, predict, classify, rank, optimise or inform a decision? | | Uncertainty | Can data, assumptions or method make the output wrong even when implementation is correct? | | Use | Does output affect business, risk, reporting, capital, customer or operational decisions? | Model classification follows substance, not software: ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Tool/model owner | Proposes classification and documents function and use | | MRM function | Challenges boundary decisions | | Business user | Identifies actual decision impact | | Internal audit | Tests classification controls | ### Permanent rule Classify the method and its use, not its technology label. "Spreadsheet", "algorithm" and "AI" do not determine model status by themselves. ### Never confuse [Model] and [Non-model tool] **Model** - uses assumptions and analytical techniques to transform inputs into estimates or decision-relevant outputs with model uncertainty. --- **Non-model tool** - performs deterministic processing without the model characteristics defined by the applicable framework, though it can still require strong controls. ### Permanent trap Treating "not a model" as "not risky". A material deterministic calculator can cause major loss even when legitimately outside the model inventory. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Definition / scope | Boundary / status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | SR 26-2: complex quantitative method using statistical/economic/financial theories on inputs for estimates. | Simple arithmetic/deterministic rules without those theories excluded. | | UK | SS1/23: quantitative methods using statistical/economic/financial/mathematical theories, techniques and assumptions. | Broader; material complex deterministic methods outside scope may still warrant MRM controls. | | EU | ECB Guide: CRR internal models. | No enterprise-wide definition. | | IN | Draft: broad input-processing-output test including internal/third-party/AI/ML systems. | Draft as at August 2026; issued 24 June 2026; consultation closed 24 July 2026. |

title: Model Risk as a Distinct Risk Type
one_screen: Model risk is the potential for adverse consequences from relying on a model whose design, data, implementation, limitations or use make its output unreliable for the decision being taken. It is distinct from the underlying risk being measured: the borrower can be unchanged while a credit model is wrong, and the market can be unchanged while a valuation model is wrong.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Object | What can go wrong | | :--- | :--- | | Underlying credit exposure | Borrower fails to pay | | Market position | Prices or rates move adversely | | Liquidity position | Cash cannot be raised when needed | | Model | The institution measures, predicts or acts on those risks incorrectly | A model can be technically sound yet still generate model risk if it is used outside its intended population, horizon or decision context. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owner | Identifies and manages model-specific risk | | Business user | Understands limitations before consuming output | | MRM / validation | Independently challenges reliability and use | | Senior management | Oversees material model risk within appetite | ### Permanent rule Model risk belongs to the use of the representation, not to the underlying exposure itself. ### Never confuse [Model risk] and [Underlying financial risk] **Model risk** - risk that reliance on a model contributes to an adverse decision or outcome. --- **Underlying financial risk** - risk inherent in the exposure or activity being modelled, such as borrower default, market movement or funding stress. ### Permanent trap Explaining an unexpected loss entirely as "credit risk" or "market risk" without asking whether the model mismeasured the risk, was used outside scope or produced misleading outputs. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The cited frameworks differ in perimeter and prescription, but all treat model risk as a risk arising from model use rather than as another name for the risk the model measures.

title: Where Model Risk Comes From
one_screen: Model risk is rarely one defect called "bad modelling". It can enter through data, assumptions, methodology, implementation, use or environmental change, and the same bad output can require a completely different remedy depending on which source failed.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Source | Failure mode | Typical control response | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Data | Wrong, incomplete, biased, stale or unrepresentative inputs | Repair lineage, quality or sampling | | Assumptions | Simplifications cease to hold | Challenge, constrain or revise assumptions | | Methodology | Model form does not represent the problem adequately | Redesign or redevelop | | Implementation | Code, configuration or interface differs from approved design | Correct implementation and retest | | Use | Output is misinterpreted or applied outside intended scope | Restrict use, train users, reapprove | | Environment | Population, behaviour or relationships change | Monitor, recalibrate or redevelop | | Governance | Weak challenge allows known limitations to persist | Escalate, remediate, strengthen control | The categories can interact: Data shift → assumption no longer holds → calibration deteriorates → users apply stale output → losses increase Root-cause analysis therefore matters more than attaching a generic "model underperformance" label. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Developer / owner | Controls design, data and implementation risks | | Model user | Controls scope, interpretation and use risk | | MRM / validation | Challenges all sources and their interactions | | Internal audit | Assesses whether the control framework catches them | ### Permanent rule A performance symptom is not a root cause. Diagnose where the failure entered before choosing the remedy. ### Never confuse [Implementation error] and [Model limitation] **Implementation error** - the production system does not execute the approved model correctly. --- **Model limitation** - the approved model itself has a known boundary, approximation or uncertainty even when implemented exactly as designed. ### Permanent trap Responding to every poor result with recalibration. Recalibration may repair stale parameter levels; it does not fix corrupted data, bad code, conceptual misspecification or misuse. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Data, design, implementation, use and environmental change are universal sources even though regulators express them with different terminology.

title: The Regulatory Perimeter: US, UK, EU and India
one_screen: There is no single global legal perimeter for MRM. The US uses broad, tailored supervisory guidance; the PRA applies SS1/23 to specified firms but across their model types; the EU prudential regime focuses on approved internal models; and India's proposed 2026 framework is broader but remains draft as at August 2026.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Jurisdiction | Institution perimeter | Model perimeter | August 2026 status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | Most relevant above USD 30bn; possible relevance below where model risk is significant | Traditional quantitative and qualifying non-generative, non-agentic AI models | Live supervisory guidance | | UK | Specified PRA firms with internal model approval | SS1/23 principles across model and risk types in those firms | Live supervisory statement | | EU | CRR institutions using permitted internal approaches | Internal credit, market and counterparty credit risk models | Live prudential framework | | IN | Eleven proposed categories of RBI-regulated entities | All models, including third-party and AI/ML | Draft; consultation closed | Entity → applicable instrument → model population → control obligations A bank may voluntarily govern more models than the legal minimum. That policy choice does not make the regulatory perimeters identical. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Separate three questions: "Is this a model?", "Is this institution in scope?", and "Does this instrument apply?" A yes to one does not answer the others. ### Permanent trap Importing one jurisdiction's requirement into another and presenting it as universal. Scope and prescription genuinely differ here. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Scope | Status / delta | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | SR 26-2/OCC Bulletin 2026-13; most relevant above USD 30bn, potentially below where model risk is significant. | Issued 17 April 2026; replaced 2011 guidance; risk-based, non-prescriptive. | | UK | Specified PRA firms with internal-model approval; new permission gives 12 months to comply; principles extend beyond approved capital models. | Current SS1/23 effective 23 April 2026. | | EU | ECB Guide covers approved CRR internal models. | Revised 28 July 2025; supervisory CRR interpretation, not enterprise MRM code. | | IN | Proposed regulatory MRM framework. | Draft as at August 2026; issued 24 June 2026; comments closed 24 July 2026; placeholder circular number invalid. |

title: Model Inventory and Dependency Map
one_screen: The model inventory is the authoritative record of what models exist, where they are in the lifecycle, who owns and uses them, and which other systems or models they depend on. A mere list of names is insufficient: the control value comes from linking identity, status, use, lineage, dependencies and governance state.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Inventory field | Control question | | :--- | :--- | | Model ID/version | Exact governed object? | | Purpose/use | Which decision depends on it? | | Owner/user | Who is accountable/consumes output? | | Risk tier | Required control intensity? | | Status | Development, validation, active, restricted, inactive or retired? | | Validation/approval | Authorised, with what conditions? | | Upstream dependencies | What can contaminate it? | | Downstream consumers | What fails if it fails? | | Third-party status | External dependency? | | Limitations/issues | Known open weaknesses? | Model A data → Model B estimate → Model C decision output Dependency mapping links inventory rows into chains, exposing propagation when upstream failure contaminates downstream models. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owner | Keeps model record accurate | | Business / technology | Confirms actual use and dependencies | | MRM function | Sets inventory standards and challenges completeness | | Internal audit | Tests completeness and reconciliation | ### Permanent rule One model has one governed identity, but it may have many uses, versions and dependencies. Inventory controls must preserve that distinction. ### Never confuse [Model inventory] and [Model repository] **Model inventory** - authoritative governance record showing models, status, ownership and control attributes. --- **Model repository** - storage location for code, documentation, artefacts or files; it may support the inventory but does not replace it. ### Permanent trap Keeping retired or restricted models invisible. Historical lineage matters for reproducing past decisions, understanding inherited outputs and managing transitions. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Inventory expectation | Scope / status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | Risk-based identification sufficient for individual and aggregate model-risk oversight; no fixed template. | 2026 guidance less prescriptive than predecessor. | | UK | SS1/23 Principle 1: identify models, maintain inventory, classify risk for proportionate controls. | Formal inventory expectation. | | EU | CRR/ECB governs prudential model scope, rating systems, changes and permissions. | No enterprise inventory mandate for every quantitative tool. | | IN | Proposed current inventory covering active, inactive, decommissioned, third-party and AI/ML models. | Draft as at August 2026; not final. |

title: Materiality and Risk Tiering
one_screen: Tiering converts model characteristics and business impact into proportional control intensity. The purpose is not to declare low-tier models harmless; it is to spend validation, approval, monitoring and governance effort where model failure can matter most while preserving a minimum control floor for every governed model.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Driver | What it captures | | :--- | :--- | | Inherent risk | Complexity, assumptions, input quality, data constraints | | Purpose | Importance of the decision or regulatory use | | Exposure | Scale of balances, customers, transactions or business affected | | Materiality | Significance of purpose plus exposure | | Consumer / operational impact | Harm beyond direct financial exposure | | Changeability | Dynamic behaviour or frequent updating | | Dependency | Whether other important models rely on it | A simple model can be high risk because its output affects a huge portfolio. A complex model can be lower materiality if it has narrow, non-critical use. Complexity and materiality therefore answer different questions. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Tiering scales controls; it never removes accountability. A lower tier means proportionate MRM, not exemption from all governance. ### Never confuse [Complexity] and [Materiality] **Complexity** - difficulty of understanding, estimating, implementing or challenging the model. --- **Materiality** - significance of the model's output to decisions and exposures. A model can be simple but highly material. ### Permanent trap Building a score that lets one benign factor cancel a critical one. A highly material model should not become "low risk" merely because its technique is simple. ### Jurisdiction variants #### US (Federal Reserve / OCC) SR 26-2 distinguishes inherent risk, model exposure and model purpose. Purpose together with exposure determines materiality; overall model risk reflects inherent risk in the context of materiality. Higher materiality warrants more rigorous oversight, while immaterial models may receive more limited controls. #### UK (PRA) SS1/23 expects firms to classify model risk and use proportionality so the level of MRM activity reflects the model's risk. The PRA does not require every firm to use the same numerical tiering scale. #### IN (RBI) As at August 2026, the RBI draft proposes risk-based tiering for all models, with materiality, complexity and other relevant factors considered collectively. The proposed tier drives validation, approval, monitoring, reporting and business-continuity intensity; high-risk models receive stronger governance. It remains draft.

title: Aggregate Model Risk and Risk Appetite
one_screen: Managing models one by one can miss the largest exposure: several individually acceptable models may rely on the same data, assumptions, vendor or economic relationship and fail together. Aggregate model risk therefore combines model-level risk with concentration and dependency, then compares that enterprise exposure with the institution's model risk appetite and tolerance.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Aggregation lens | Example question | | :--- | :--- | | Common data | How many models depend on the same customer master or market feed? | | Common methodology | Would one invalid assumption impair several models? | | Model chains | Does an upstream output feed many downstream decisions? | | Vendor concentration | Could one provider outage or defect affect many models? | | Business concentration | Are critical decisions clustered around a small model set? | | Technology concentration | Do several models share one platform or implementation layer? | Risk appetite states how much model risk the institution is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives. Tolerance converts that high-level appetite into actionable boundaries, escalation triggers or control expectations. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owners | Report model-level risk and dependencies | | Enterprise MRM | Aggregates risk and identifies concentration | | Senior management | Operates within approved appetite | | Board / relevant committee | Oversees appetite and material breaches | ### Permanent rule Portfolio diversification of financial exposures does not guarantee diversification of model risk. Shared models, data and assumptions can create hidden common-mode failure. ### Never confuse [Model tier] and [Model risk appetite] **Model tier** - classification of one model used to scale its controls. --- **Model risk appetite** - enterprise statement of how much model risk the institution is prepared to accept and under what constraints. ### Permanent trap Adding model risk scores as though they were independent. Aggregation must recognise dependencies and correlated failure, not just arithmetic totals. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The exact appetite framework is institution-specific, but assessing model risk both individually and in aggregate and governing material exposures is a common MRM principle.

title: The Model Lifecycle and Its Control Gates
one_screen: A model lifecycle is not a project plan; it is a sequence of governed states in which evidence must be sufficient before the model can move forward. The key control idea is the gate: development does not grant use, validation does not grant approval, approval does not end monitoring, and change can reopen earlier gates.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Gate | Minimum decision | | :--- | :--- | | Development complete | Is the evidence pack sufficient for independent challenge? | | Validation complete | Is the model reliable enough for its intended use, with known limitations? | | Approval | Is residual model risk acceptable and use authorised? | | Deployment | Does production reproduce the approved model? | | Monitoring | Does evidence still support continued use? | | Change | Does the change reopen validation or approval? | | Retirement | Can use cease without breaking dependencies or records? | Lifecycle controls are recursive. A material change can return an active model to development, validation and approval rather than allowing an informal production patch. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owner | Coordinates the model through lifecycle stages | | Developer | Produces development and change evidence | | Validation / MRM | Independently challenges relevant stages | | Approval authority | Authorises use and material changes | | Business user | Operates only within approved conditions | ### Permanent rule A lifecycle stage creates evidence; a gate creates authority. Evidence from one stage is not authority to skip the next. ### Never confuse [Validation] and [Approval] **Validation** - independent assessment of reliability, limitations and fitness for intended use. --- **Approval** - governance decision to accept residual risk and authorise specified use, possibly with conditions. ### Permanent trap Treating "live" as the final state. Production use begins a new control phase in which monitoring, issue management, change and eventual retirement remain governed. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The cited regimes use different language and degrees of prescription, but the lifecycle logic of development, challenge, approval, use, monitoring, change and exit is common.

title: Who Produces, Uses, Approves, Challenges and Audits
one_screen: Ownership is the load-bearing control in MRM because the same person should not create evidence, decide whether that evidence is convincing, accept the residual risk and audit the process. Effective governance separates production, consumption, approval, independent challenge and assurance while ensuring the challenger has expertise, standing and access to decision-makers.
